title: Reclaiming Your Birthright
text:
Rabbi Zalman Goldstein tells this story of an estate sale in Monsey, New York.

I walked into an estate sale. The owner was an elderly woman, and her children were running it. In the middle of the room sat a ceramic matzah dish and two brass candlesticks. I didn't pay much attention to them at the time. I began to feel a sadness: all these items were fifty or sixty years of memories, now laid out for anyone to see and buy. Eventually I found something to buy just to make the owners happy. On the way out, the older woman, the owner of the house, wished me "Good Shabbos."

As soon as I left, I realized I had missed an opportunity. I couldn't stop thinking about those candlesticks. I stopped at the bakery and picked up a fresh challah and a bottle of wine, picked up my children from school and told them the mission. We came back. Whew! The candlesticks were still there. I found the older woman and asked her if the candlesticks were for sale. "Eight dollars for the pair." "Deal."

The son went to the table, took the candlesticks and put them in my hands. "Here!" I held them, my kids watching my every move. Then I turned to the mother, looked her softly in the eye and said, "Do you know why I came all the way back and bought these candlesticks?"

"No."

"I came back together with my children to buy them from you, so that we could give them back to you. We want these candlesticks to stay in your dining room and keep lighting up your home every Friday night and holiday night."

Tears welled up in her eyes. Mine soon followed. Our daughter Hindy gave her the bag with the candles and glass holders. Moishy gave her the challah. Chana gave her the wine. The woman's son and daughter froze, and tears came to their eyes too. "We used to light these years ago," they said. "We used to do this every Friday night." There were hugs and tears between them. She warmly accepted our gift, and assured us that she "already knows the beracha," the blessing.

The moral of the story: when you give a Jew a Shabbat candle, you're not giving them anything new. You're giving them back their own candles. When you pick up a pair of tefillin and put them on, they are already yours; they have been in your family for a hundred generations. When you go to shul, you're simply going home. When you talk to G-d in prayer, you're talking to your Father. When you study Torah or celebrate Shabbat, you're not trying something new, some "religious activity." You're taking back what is already yours. You're reclaiming your birthright.
source: Chabad.org, "A Strange Estate Sale Transaction" by Rabbi Zalman Goldstein

title: What Was in the Rebbe's Bags
text:
One of my earliest Rosh Hashanah memories is from the late 1980s. I was about eleven years old, in the synagogue of the Lubavitcher Rebbe. The shul was packed; people were singing and praying and swaying to the melodies. The Rebbe was ready to blow the shofar. He stood on a raised platform in the center of the synagogue, and a palpable rush of energy filled the room.

As I scanned the room, I noticed large bags in front of him, filled with something mysterious. The Rebbe covered the bags with the top of his tallit and stood bent over them. You could hear him sobbing from under the tallit. I wondered what was in those bags.

I turned to a knowledgeable fellow beside me and asked, "What's in those brown paper bags? Is it a mystical text, or some sacred object?"

"No, nothing so lofty," he said. "Those bags are filled with letters from people across the world, asking for blessings for the New Year. Letters from people going through every difficulty imaginable: health issues, family issues, financial issues. Letters filled with pain and longing."

It dawned on me that in the final moments before the sounding of the shofar, the Rebbe was thinking about people's mortgages and hospital bills and special needs, and praying for them.
source: Shabbos House (Rabbi Mendel Rubin), 'The Rebbe's Shofar: Rising from the Brown Paper Bags'; Chassidishe Derher on the bags of panim under the Rebbe's tallis

title: Tear Up the Telegram
text:
Shortly after Sol Teichman's Bar Mitzvah in 1940, his father was taken away to a Hungarian labor camp. On the second day of Passover 1944, all the Jews of Munkacz were given one hour to leave their homes and were herded into ghettos. In June they were transported to Auschwitz. That was the last time Sol saw his mother, his sister and three of his brothers. "If you didn't have hope, prayers, belief in G-d, you had nothing to live for," Mr. Teichman says.

He wouldn't eat on Yom Kippur, he shared his meager rations with others, and even though his weight dropped to sixty pounds, Sol Teichman stayed strong.

As the end of the war approached, the Nazis forced many of their Jewish prisoners on the infamous death march to Dachau. Sol and his brother Steve began the march. Steve's strength gave out, so Sol carried him for the rest of the way. Of the 6,000 who started the march, only about 600 survived, Sol and his brother among them. "It never leaves you; it stays with you all the time," Mr. Teichman says years later, shaking his head. He still cannot comprehend how anyone survived. "It never leaves you; it stays with you all the time," he repeats.

At one point, as the war was drawing to a close, Sol, his brother, a cousin and many others were loaded onto a train to be killed. But the Allies began bombing and the train stopped. Not wanting to take any chances, everyone jumped off and ran down the steep slope beside the tracks. Sol and Steve lost track of their cousin, and each assumed the other had perished.

The war finally ended. Sol and Steve went to Budapest to look for their father. They walked into a store, and not two minutes later, in walked their cousin. It was an especially poignant reunion, since the cousin had already told their father that his sons were not alive. Their time together was brief. Their father, who was supporting himself selling goods on the black market, was reported to the authorities and arrested.

Sol and Steve were alone again. They registered with the United States government, hoping their American relatives would serve as sponsors. They were chosen to be among the 200 orphans sponsored by Eleanor Roosevelt to enter the US, the first children out of Europe. We often call a child with only one remaining parent an orphan, but that was apparently not the government's definition. As the ship was about to leave port, the captain received a telegram: "Take off the Teichman children immediately; their father is alive; they are not orphans."

Sol and Steve were found and brought, shivering and sobbing, to the captain's office. Since they spoke only Yiddish, an interpreter was called. "What are they going to do to us?" the terrified boys kept asking. The captain was moved by their plight. "What am I going to do?" he said. "Punish these young children because their father is alive? Tear up the telegram."

The Teichman brothers set sail for America. The boat docked in New York on a Shabbat afternoon, and Sol and his brother refused to get off until Shabbat had ended. The voice of the Minchas Elazar was ringing in their ears: "Keep the Shabbos and it will be good for you."

It took three long years for their father to join them in America, three years of working and scrimping and sending every extra cent to relatives in Europe. Together with their father, the Teichmans moved to Los Angeles, and a new life began.
source: Naaleh.com, Torat Imecha vol. 8 no. 25, 'The Saga of Heroic Children: Shlomo Zalman Teichman' (Rabbi Hanoch Teller); Simon Wiesenthal Center obituary

title: The Power of the Siddur
text:
The famous Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal, who died in 2005, once spoke at a conference of European rabbis in Bratislava, Slovakia. The rabbis presented the 91-year-old Wiesenthal with an award, and Mr. Wiesenthal, visibly moved, told them the following story.

It was in Mauthausen, shortly after liberation. The camp was visited by Rabbi Eliezer Silver, head of the Agudas Harabonim, the Union of Orthodox Rabbis of North America, on a mission to bring aid and comfort to the survivors. Rabbi Silver organized a special prayer service and invited Wiesenthal to join the other survivors in prayer.

Mr. Wiesenthal declined, and explained why. "In the camp," he said to Rabbi Silver, "there was one religious man who somehow managed to smuggle in a siddur, a prayer book. At first I greatly admired him for his courage, for risking his life to bring the siddur in. But the next day I realized, to my horror, that this man was 'renting out' the siddur to people in exchange for food. People were giving him their last piece of bread for a few minutes with the prayer book. This man, who was thin and emaciated when it all started, was soon eating so much that he died before everyone else; his system couldn't handle it."

Mr. Wiesenthal continued: "If this is how religious Jews behave, I'm not going to have anything to do with a prayer book." And he turned to walk away.

Rabbi Silver touched him on the shoulder and said gently, in Yiddish, "Oy, na'ar, na'ar, silly boy. Why do you look at the Jew who used his siddur to take food out of starving people's mouths? Why don't you look at the many Jews who gave up their last piece of bread in order to use a siddur? That's faith. That's the true power of the siddur."

Rabbi Silver then embraced him. "I went to the services the next day," said Wiesenthal.

Not everything is as it seems at first glance. G-d wants us to look deeper.
source: Chabad.org (KabbalaOnline), 'Switched Perspective' (Yosef Ben-Shlomo HaKohein); NCSY, 'The Last Piece of Bread'

title: The Vizhnitzer Rebbe's Silent Visit
text:
Every weekday evening, Rabbi Yisroel Hager, the saintly Vizhnitzer Rebbe, would go out for a stroll of about half an hour, accompanied by one of his attendants.

One day, to the surprise of his shammes, the Rebbe stopped in front of a large house just before the park. It belonged to the manager of the town bank. The Rebbe went up the steps and knocked on the door. The shammes had no idea what the Rebbe could possibly want in this house. The bank manager was most certainly not a chassid; in fact, he was one of the local leaders of the Haskalah. Nevertheless, when he saw the door open and the butler usher the Rebbe in, the shammes quickly raced up the steps and slipped into the house too, not willing to leave the Rebbe alone and unattended.

The bank manager came downstairs and couldn't believe his eyes: the Vizhnitzer Rebbe, in his house! He greeted his guest warmly, showed him to a comfortable chair in the salon, and sat down opposite him.

After some initial pleasantries, he waited for the Rebbe to state the reason for his unexpected call. A few minutes passed, in silence. The host became a little uncomfortable. A refined, cosmopolitan man, he would never presume to confront his distinguished guest about why he had come. Excusing himself, he walked to a spot where the Rebbe couldn't see him and frantically signaled to the shammes to join him in the hall.

"Why on earth did the Rabbi come here?"

"I have no idea. The Rebbe didn't tell me anything. I saw him enter, so I followed him in."

Perplexed, the bank manager resumed his seat. He looked at the Rebbe. The Rebbe looked at him. More silence. What was going on? The host found his sophisticated restraint strained to the utmost.

Finally, after several more minutes, the Rebbe stood up. Still without a word, he walked toward the door. Displaying good manners, the bank manager escorted him out. He followed the Rebbe down the steps and several paces along the sidewalk, then started to turn back, but almost instantly reconsidered and kept following behind the calmly strolling tzaddik.

When they reached the Rebbe's house and the Rebbe paused to start up the steps, the bank manager finally threw off all restraint and called out, "Vizhnitzer Rebbe! Please excuse me for asking, but why did you come to my house? While you were my guest I would never presume to pry, but now we are at your house, so I can ask."

The Rebbe turned slowly toward him. "I came to your house to fulfill a mitzvah. Thank G-d, I succeeded."

"Which mitzvah?"

"Our sages say that just as it is a mitzvah to speak out when you will be listened to, so it is a mitzvah not to say anything when you know you will not be listened to. But what does it mean, not to say anything?" the Rebbe continued. "To sit in your own house in silence? Not at all. You have to go to the other person, and then not say anything! And that," concluded the Rebbe, "is what I did."

"So what is it that you did not say?" asked the bewildered bank manager.

"I can't tell you that."

"Why not?"

"Because then I will lose my mitzvah!"

"But how do you know that I wouldn't listen?"

"I know."

"But you can't know that. You must tell me what it is!" pleaded the bank manager, totally overcome by curiosity.

"I'm sorry. No," said the Rebbe firmly.

After several more rounds, the bank manager begged, "Please, please, please, at least give me a chance."

"Oh, all right," said the Rebbe, with a show of reluctance. "Yesterday a distraught woman, recently widowed, came to speak to me. She had received a notice from your bank that it has decided to put her house up for auction next week because she owes so much on the mortgage. That means she and her little children will be out on the street. She asked me, as the rabbinical leader of the town, to speak to you, because she knows that you are Jewish. She hoped I could influence you to be compassionate. I, however, did not bring it up to you, because of the mitzvah not to say something that will be ignored."

"But Rebbe," cried the bank manager in frustration, "you don't understand! It's not me she owes, it's the bank. And I don't own the bank, I only manage it. I don't set policy. Besides..."

"Right," the Rebbe interrupted. "As I said. I knew you wouldn't listen. Good night."

The Rebbe walked up the steps to his home, followed by his shammes. The door closed behind them. The bank manager stood there, stunned. Finally he walked home, alone and bemused. But the matter had entered his heart, and he was unable to dismiss it. Before the week was out, he paid the widow's entire mortgage out of his own personal account.
source: KabbalaOnline.org (Chabad), 'Silence Speaks' (from Sippurei Chassidim); Chabad.org 'Silence Speaks' (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: A Life for a Life: Dr. Gisella Perl
text:
We all know about the infamous Angel of Death, Dr. Josef Mengele, who stood at Auschwitz and, with one finger pointing right or left, personally decided the fate of countless Jews as they arrived. One way meant work and a chance at life. The other was a death sentence, and before long all that remained of those people was ashes.

Chaya was a young bride, married at nineteen. She didn't have much of a honeymoon, because soon after her wedding she and her husband found themselves in Auschwitz. Her new husband was sent one way and she the other, and it didn't take long for Chaya to realize that she was now a very young widow. A short while later she realized something else: she was carrying more than memories. She was carrying a child.

As soon as she shared the news, the women in the barracks warned her. "As soon as the Nazis find out you're pregnant, you're dead. And not only dead: Dr. Mengele will torture you and the baby with his medical experiments, and then you'll both be burned." Chaya wanted this child so badly, as a memorial to its father, but the women were adamant that in Auschwitz a pregnancy was a double death sentence. "Then what should I do?" she cried. "Don't worry, Chaya. We'll call Dr. Perl. She will look after you."

Dr. Gisella Perl, born and educated in Sighet, Transylvania, was now an inmate in Auschwitz. She was a gynecologist and obstetrician, and she was known as "the other doctor at Auschwitz." Where Mengele killed, Perl cured. He sent people to hell; she brought them healing, as best she could under the most impossible of circumstances.

Dr. Perl examined Chaya. "You are too far along now for an abortion," she told her. "We must hide your pregnancy, and when the time comes, I will do what I have to do to save your life." Chaya was young and still naive about life in Auschwitz. The older women had to explain to her that here there was simply no choice: Dr. Perl would have to deliver the baby and then suffocate it, otherwise mother and child would both be butchered.

The dreaded time came, and Chaya was taken into the latrine, crying, "Please save my baby. I'm begging you, Doctor, please!"

"Chaya'le, I too am a woman. I too am a Jew," said Dr. Perl. "And as a doctor and an obstetrician, I am committed to bringing life into the world. But tragically, this is the only way we can save your life. Every time the Nazis find a pregnant woman it's the same: double torture and double death. At least this way we can hope to save the mothers' lives. But Chaya'le, I promise you: if we ever get out of this hell, I will dedicate myself to bringing life into the world."

Miraculously, Chaya survived, and eventually she came to New York. In the 1950s she was living in Borough Park, then a fledgling Jewish neighborhood. She remarried, thank G-d, and before long she was expecting, and busy looking for an obstetrician.

One day, walking down the street in Borough Park, she noticed a sign: "Dr. G. Perl, Obstetrician." Could it be? Was it possible? Could this really be the same Dr. Perl from Auschwitz? Had she survived too, and did she live here as well? Chaya ran inside the building, looking for Dr. Perl's office. She opened the door and froze. Instantly the two women recognized each other and flew into each other's arms. They embraced and wept for a long time.

"Will you keep your promise to me?" asked Chaya. "I want you to deliver my baby!"

This time it was not in the filthy latrine of Auschwitz but in a clean, sterile delivery room at Maimonides Hospital in Brooklyn. As Dr. Perl brought Chaya's baby into the world, she shouted the words that became her trademark, her slogan and her battle cry every time she delivered a Jewish baby: "A life for a life!" In Auschwitz she had been forced to take life away; now, in America, she was restoring it. "Mazel tov! It's a boy! L'chaim, to life!"

"Yes," said Chaya. "I will call him Chaim, for Life."

It is estimated that over the war years Dr. Perl saved the lives of some 10,000 Jewish women in Auschwitz. And through the years, every time she delivered a Jewish baby, she shouted those words: "A life for a life!" She passed away in 1984. May her special soul rest in peace.

On Yom Kippur, we too want to shout: "A life for a life!"
source: The Jewish Star, Rabbi Binny Freedman, 'It's not what's lost, but what's to be achieved' (Isralight); background: History.com on Dr. Gisella Perl

title: Paid in Full With One Glass of Milk
text:
Dr. Howard Kelly was a distinguished physician at Johns Hopkins.

According to his biographer, Audrey Davis, the doctor was on a walking trip through northern Pennsylvania one spring day when he stopped at a farmhouse for a drink of water. A little girl answered his knock at the door and, instead of water, brought him a glass of fresh milk. He visited with her briefly, then went on his way.

Some time later, the little girl came to him as a patient and needed surgery. After the surgery, the bill was brought to her room, and on it were the words: "Paid in full with one glass of milk."
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: Reb Aryeh Levin's Etrog
text:
Reb Aryeh Levin, of sacred memory, was renowned as a righteous man of Jerusalem. He was known for his meticulous observance of every one of the commandments, and for his overwhelming compassion for every human being.

Two days before Sukkot, he went to the Geula neighborhood of Jerusalem to choose his Four Species. Word spread immediately that the great tzaddik Reb Aryeh was standing in front of a long table in the street, selecting his species, and a large crowd gathered around him. After all, the Torah calls the etrog "the fruit of a beautiful tree," and since we are told to beautify the commandments, observant Jews take special care to buy the most beautiful and outstanding etrog they can.

Everyone wanted to see which criteria the great tzaddik would use in choosing his etrog. To the crowd's amazement, Reb Aryeh looked at one etrog and put it down, picked up a second and examined it, then went back to the first and bought it, together with his three other species. The whole transaction took less than five minutes.

The disappointed crowd quickly dispersed, imagining that the great rabbi must have had a very pressing appointment. One man decided to follow Reb Aryeh to see exactly where he was going. "What could be more important than choosing an etrog the day before Sukkot?" this Jerusalemite thought to himself. Reb Aryeh walked into an old-age home. The man waited outside, and ninety minutes later the great sage came out.

The Jerusalemite approached him. "Revered Rabbi," he said, "please don't think me impudent, but I am anxious to learn a point of Torah, and so I ask: the great commandment of Sukkot includes the waving of a beautiful etrog. I am certain that visiting the elderly in the old-age home is also an important mitzvah, but they will be there during Sukkot and after it too. Buying the etrog is a once-a-year opportunity. I would have expected the revered rabbi to spend a little more time choosing his etrog."

Reb Aryeh took the questioner's hand in his and smiled lovingly. "My dear friend," he said, "there are two mitzvot for which the Torah uses the word *hidur*, beautification. One is the mitzvah of a beautiful etrog, *pri etz hadar* (Leviticus 23:40). The second is honoring the face of the aged, *ve'hadarta pnei zaken* (Leviticus 19:32). But the etrog is an object, and the aged person is a human being, not a fruit. So I believe one must spend much more time beautifying the commandment that concerns a human being than the one that concerns a fruit."
source: The Jerusalem Post (Judaism magazine), Reb Aryeh Levin etrog story; also The Jewish Education Project and Times of Israel (Rabbi Elie Weinstock)

title: Ben-Gurion and the Mayflower
text:
David Ben-Gurion was once challenged by a foreign statesman: "Tell me, Mr. Ben-Gurion, who do you and your state represent? The Jews of Poland? Of Yemen, Romania, Morocco, Iraq, Russia, or perhaps Brazil? After two thousand years of exile, can you honestly speak of a single nation, a single culture? Can you speak of a single heritage, a single Jewish tradition?"

Ben-Gurion answered him: "Look, sir. About three hundred years ago, the Mayflower set sail from England, carrying the first settlers of what would become the largest democratic superpower in the world, the United States of America. Now, do me a favor. Go out into the street, find ten American children, and ask them: What was the name of the captain of the Mayflower? How long did the voyage take? What did the people on the ship eat? What were the conditions at sea during the voyage? I'm sure you would agree with me that there is a good chance you won't get a good answer to these questions.

"Now, in contrast: not three hundred but more than three thousand years ago, the Jews left the land of Egypt. I would kindly ask you, sir, on one of your trips around the world, to try to meet ten Jewish children in different countries and ask them: What was the name of the leader who took the Jews out of Egypt? How long did it take them to reach the land of Israel? What did they eat while they wandered in the desert? And what happened to the sea when they came to it? Once you have the answers to these questions, please carefully reconsider the question you have just asked me."
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: The Honors Class That Wasn't
text:
Jennie Ivey, fresh out of teaching college, got a job teaching history at an inner-city high school. To her surprise, she was given the honors class.

When the students filed in on the first day of school with attitude, she assumed they resented being assigned a rookie teacher. She decided to treat them with the respect they deserved, and told them what an honor it was for her to teach the honors class.

She spent the entire first period asking for their guidance: what did they *not* like about history? As the students shared their pet peeves, Jennie took careful notes. That night she went home and built her strategy. Her classes would have no lists of names, places and dates, and no multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank tests. She would teach history with relevance to current events, and explore the hearts and minds of the real people who lived all those years ago.

The students responded to her efforts and thrived in her class. The discussions were lively, the subjects engaging and the atmosphere light. Her classes were so enjoyable that the students looked forward to them all day. They were so enthusiastic that they entered national competitions and brought home a trophy. The days and months rolled by so fast that she couldn't believe the end of the year had already arrived.

On the last day of the year, the principal commended her work with the remedial class. Jennie was confused. None of her classes were remedial; they were all honors. The principal pointed out that her history class in period A was remedial, but Jennie showed the principal her copy of the class list, and across the top the word "Honors" was clearly marked. They were both in shock. Jennie really hadn't known she was teaching a remedial class. She had treated them like an honors class, and they rose to the challenge.

Jennie learned a lesson that day that is never taught in teaching college. There is no such thing as a remedial student. It all depends on how you treat them. Treat them like honor students, and they will find their honor.
source: Jennie Ivey, 'The Honors Class', in Chicken Soup for the Soul: The Power of Positive (2012); summarized in SEEN Magazine, Winter 2022

title: The Milkman and the Baker
text:
Early one morning, a milkman was bewildered to find a court summons hanging on his door. He was an honest man and had always behaved as one. He never cheated, lied or stole. He had no idea why he had been summoned to court.

But the baker knew. The baker used to buy butter and cheese from the milkman for his business. One day he began to suspect that the lumps of butter the milkman sold him weighed less than five pounds, even though the milkman insisted that each was exactly five pounds. The baker decided to look into it, and for a while he weighed every lump of butter he bought from the milkman. He found that they were indeed less than five pounds. Sometimes four pounds, sometimes four and a half, and once even three. The baker was angry. "He's cheating me!" he told his wife. "I am not going to keep quiet about it."

He went to the local court and complained about the milkman. "We have to prosecute him," said the baker. "We can't let him cheat all the villagers. People trust this crook!" Later that day, the court messenger hung a notice on the milkman's house summoning him to court.

The milkman arrived at the courthouse shaking with fear. He had never been to a court and had never spoken to a judge, and the judge was a man the villagers feared.

"I assume you have a very accurate scale in your dairy," the judge said to the milkman.

"No, Your Honor, I do not have a scale," said the milkman.

"So how do you weigh the butter? Do you just guess?"

"No, G-d forbid, Your Honor. I am an honest man; it would never occur to me to do something like that. Very simply, I built myself a scale, the kind that needs a weight on one side to balance the butter on the other."

The judge nodded, and the milkman continued. "Every morning, when I come to weigh the butter for the baker, I place the five-pound loaf of bread he gives me on one side of the scale. That way I know that the butter I give the baker will be exactly five pounds."

"So," said the judge, "you're telling us that the butter you give the baker weighs exactly as much as the loaf of bread he supplies to you?"

"That is exactly it!" exclaimed the milkman.

The baker's face fell. You see, the baker's own scale was dishonest. The five pounds of bread he weighed out each morning for the milkman were not truly five pounds, and that is exactly what came back to him.

How true this is of many of us. We judge people based on who we are, and what we put out to people is what comes back to us. In life, we end up eating the cake we ourselves have baked.
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: A Thousand Marbles
text:
The older I get, the more I enjoy Sunday mornings. Perhaps it's the quiet solitude that comes with being the first to rise, or maybe it's the unbounded joy of not having to be at work. Either way, the first few hours of a Sunday morning are a pleasure.

A few weeks ago, I was shuffling toward the kitchen with a steaming cup of coffee in one hand and the morning paper in the other. What began as a typical Sunday morning turned into one of those lessons that life hands you from time to time. Let me tell you about it.

I turned up the volume on my radio to listen to a Sunday morning talk show, and heard an older-sounding man with a golden voice, the kind who sounds as if he should be in broadcasting himself. He was talking about "a thousand marbles" to someone named Tom.

I was intrigued, and sat down to listen. "Well, Tom, it sure sounds like you're busy with your job. I'm sure they pay you well, but it's a shame you have to be away from home and your family so much. Hard to believe a young fellow should have to work sixty or seventy hours a week to make ends meet. Too bad you missed your daughter's dance recital.

"Let me tell you something, Tom, something that has helped me keep a good perspective on my own priorities." And that's when he began to explain his theory of a thousand marbles.

"You see, I sat down one day and did a little arithmetic. The average person lives about seventy-five years. I know, some live more and some live less, but on average, folks live about seventy-five years. Now then, I multiplied 75 by 52 and came up with 3,900, which is the number of Sundays the average person has in an entire lifetime. Now stick with me, Tom, I'm getting to the important part.

"It took me until I was fifty-five years old to think about all this in any detail, and by then I had lived through more than twenty-eight hundred Sundays. I got to thinking that if I lived to be seventy-five, I only had about a thousand of them left to enjoy. So I went to a toy store and bought every single marble they had. I ended up having to visit three toy stores to round up a thousand marbles. I took them home and put them in a large, clear plastic container right here in my workshop, next to the radio. Every Sunday since then, I have taken one marble out and thrown it away.

"I found that by watching the marbles diminish, I focused more on the really important things in life. There is nothing like watching your time on this earth run out to help you get your priorities straight.

"Now let me tell you one last thing before I sign off and take my lovely wife out to breakfast. This morning, I took the very last marble out of the container. I figure that if I make it to next Sunday, I have been given a little extra time. And the one thing we can all use is a little more time.

"It was nice to talk to you, Tom. I hope you spend more time with your loved ones, and I hope to meet you again someday. Have a good morning!"

You could have heard a pin drop when he finished. Even the show's host didn't have anything to say for a few moments. I guess he gave us all a lot to think about. I had planned to do some work that morning, then go to the gym. Instead, I went upstairs and woke my wife with a kiss. "Come on, honey, I'm taking you and the kids to breakfast."

"What brought this on?" she asked with a smile.

"Oh, nothing special. It's just been a long time since we spent a Sunday together with the kids. Hey, can we stop at a toy store while we're out? I need to buy some marbles."
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: Eight Candles at the Border
text:
Shortly after Kristallnacht, in 1938, a Jewish family from Berlin, the Geiers, was trying to escape Germany on a train bound for Holland. They worried that the Gestapo agents at the border would find fault with their papers and find an excuse to detain them. It was the last night of Chanukah, and the family had not had a chance to light the Chanukah candles.

When they arrived at the border, a long line of Gestapo agents boarded the train. But just as they began to examine the passports, the lights in the entire station went out. The father of the Jewish family pulled out his menorah and quickly lit eight candles, one after the other. The lights attracted unwanted attention, and the little compartment quickly filled with unsmiling Gestapo agents. But the agents paid the Jews no attention. They simply used the candlelight to do their job, inspecting the passports of the train's passengers. When the last passport had been examined, the agents turned to the Jewish family and checked their papers, which were in order, and the chief thanked them politely for their "travel candles."

As soon as the agents left the train, the lights in the whole station came back on, and the train crossed the border.
source: Arnold Geier (son of Judah Geier), in 'Small Miracles of the Holocaust' (Halberstam & Leventhal), reprinted on Chabad.org ('Travel Candles') and Aish.com

title: Reb Mendel and the Pickpocket
text:
Reb Mendel Futerfas, a chassid with a long white beard, was arrested for helping to smuggle Jews out of the Soviet Union. He sat in a Gulag camp in Siberia, housed in a barrack full of gangsters.

The gangsters played cards, a pastime forbidden in the Gulag. So they posted a lookout at the door, and whenever the guards came, the alarm was raised and the cards were hidden. The guards knew about the card games, but try as they might, they could never find the evidence. A guard would burst into the room and search every nook and cranny, and somehow the cards always eluded him. Reb Mendel did his best to watch the gangsters and discover where the cards were hidden, but he never managed to spot the hiding place.

One day Reb Mendel asked one of the gangsters where the cards were hidden, and the gangster explained the secret. "Among us," he said, "there is a master pickpocket. We pass the cards to him, and as soon as the guard enters, the pickpocket slips them into the guard's back pocket. The guard looks everywhere for the cards, but he can't find them, because he already has them."

"And, pray tell," asked Reb Mendel, "how do you get them back?"

"That's simple," replied the gangster. "Just before the guard leaves, the pickpocket takes them back."

Whenever Reb Mendel retold this story he would have a good laugh, and then he would grow serious and explain the moral; Reb Mendel's stories always came with a moral. The moral of this one: when you criticize others, make sure to check yourself first. You may well be the guilty party.
source: Chabad.org, 'Pickpockets' (The Rebbe section) and 'The Rabbi and the Thief'; Reb Mendel Futerfas, 'My Gulag Life'

title: An Expert in Souls
text:
A diamond merchant once came to the Rebbe Rashab and asked him why he spent so much time on simple people.

The Rebbe asked the merchant whether he had any diamonds with him. The chassid pulled out a pouch and spread some diamonds on the table. When the Rebbe said that he saw nothing special about them, the chassid replied, "If you'll excuse me, Rebbe, one has to be an expert to tell a truly fine gem from a flawed one."

The Rebbe responded, "A Jew is also a gem, and you have to be an expert in souls to tell them apart."
source: Chabad.org, 'The Diamond Merchant' (from Sefer HaSichos 5705, p. 41) (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: The Horse Never Spoke
text:
He was a noted scholar who had accomplished much in his years of Torah study. Now he had discovered, in an obscure book of Kabbalah, that if a suitable person went forty days and forty nights without uttering a single unnecessary word, he would merit Divine inspiration. Excited, he decided to attempt it. He spent as much of the time as he could studying Torah and avoided company as much as he was able. The forty days passed without mishap, and he exhaled in relief. Then his breath grew short again, as he began to tremble in anticipation of the blessed revelation.

After the evening prayer he shut himself in his room and waited. And waited. And waited. He could not understand it. What had gone wrong? He knew with certainty that he had not failed the requirement. Had he miscounted the days? But another day and night went by, and another, and another, and still nothing happened. How could this be?

He decided to travel to the chassidic rebbe he had heard so much about, Rabbi Yisrael, the holy Ruzhiner. When he arrived, he was astonished by what he saw. The Rebbe lived in extraordinary luxury! The house, the furnishings, the clothing, everything was of the most expensive materials, fit for the highest aristocracy. Was this any way for a spiritual leader to live, and a chassidic rebbe no less? He wondered whether he had made a mistake in coming, and as the days passed he became convinced of it. How could a man who lived in such opulence have anything to tell him about Divine inspiration? He decided to go home without even speaking to the so-called holy master.

As he passed the Ruzhiner's house, he saw the Rebbe come out. Four magnificent white horses were harnessed to a carriage worthy of royalty. As the Rebbe was about to climb to his seat, he paused and patted one of the horses on the head, three times.

This was too much for the frustrated scholar. He dashed over to the Rebbe and challenged him: "Explain to me, please, exalted sir, what spiritual work a chassidic master is engaged in while he is petting a horse?"

The Ruzhiner looked at him a moment and answered gently, "Ah, but you do not understand. This special horse has just completed forty days and nights without uttering an unnecessary word."
source: KabbalaOnline.org (Chabad), 'Forty Days and Forty Nights' (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: True Kavanah: The Master Key
text:
Finally the great moment arrived. It was the morning of Rosh Hashanah, and Rabbi Ze'ev stood on the bimah in the center of the Baal Shem Tov's synagogue, among the Torah scrolls, surrounded by a sea of men wrapped in their tallitot. At his table in the southeast corner of the room stood his master, the Baal Shem Tov, his face aflame. An awed silence filled the room in anticipation of the climax of the day: the piercing blasts and sobs of the shofar.

Rabbi Ze'ev reached into his pocket and his heart froze. The paper had disappeared! He distinctly remembered putting it there that morning, but now it was gone. Furiously he searched his memory for the kavanot, the mystical intentions he had learned, but his distress over the lost notes seemed to have paralyzed his mind. It was a total blank. Tears of frustration filled his eyes. He had disappointed his master, who had entrusted him with this most sacred task. He would have to blow the shofar like a simple horn, without any kavanot.

With a despairing heart, Rabbi Ze'ev blew the sounds required by halachah and, avoiding his master's eye, went back to his place. When the day's prayers were over, the Baal Shem Tov made his way to the corner where Rabbi Ze'ev sat sobbing under his tallit.

"Gut Yom Tov, Reb Ze'ev!" he called. "That was a most extraordinary shofar blowing we heard today!"

"But Rebbe... why...?"

"In the king's palace," said Rabbi Yisrael, "there are many gates and doors, leading to many halls and chambers. The palace keepers carry great rings holding many keys, each of which opens a different door. But there is a master key that opens all the doors. The kavanot are keys; each unlocks a door and opens another chamber in the upper worlds. But there is one key that unlocks every door and can open the innermost chambers of the Divine palace. That master key is a broken heart."
source: Chabad.org, 'The Master Key: A Broken Heart' (Baal Shem Tov and Rabbi Ze'ev Kitzes) (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: Rabbi Sacks's First Sukkah
text:
Rabbi Jonathan Sacks writes: I remember when I built my first sukkah. It was almost a catastrophe. It happened like this. My wife and I were newly married and had just settled into our new home.

One morning, leaving the synagogue, a friend said, "I'm just off to the local timber yard to buy wood to build a sukkah. Would you like to come with me?" Delightedly, I said yes. We didn't have a car, and I had been wondering how to buy and carry home the materials for a hut. The offer was providential. We went back to his home to get the list of things he needed. The contrast between us could not have been greater. My friend, who was later to become one of Anglo-Jewry's great rabbis, was superbly organized. He had drawn up architectural plans for his temporary dwelling. It was to be a stand-alone structure with windows and a door, and it would need considerable skill in carpentry. He had made a long and precise list of materials and was ready to begin.

I was shame-faced. I had no idea how to make anything, let alone a sukkah. In school I had always come bottom of the class in woodworking, and when it came to practical things, changing a light bulb was the limit of my ability. Humbled, I followed him into the car, hoping inspiration would come. At the timber yard he rattled off his list and ended up with an impressive pile of beams and planks and hinges and screws. I settled for an improvised list: a few sheets of hardboard, some wooden supports and a bag of nails.

We went off to our homes and began hammering away. Before the festival began we visited each other to see the results. His was a thing of beauty, a summer house in which anyone could have faced wandering in the wilderness with equanimity. Ours was modest by any standard. I had joined the hardboard to the beams to make three square walls, nailed them to one another, and rested them against the back wall of the house. It looked like a large packing case. There was a hole for a door.

The festival arrived, and as luck would have it, there was a storm on the second night. The wind howled and blew itself into a gale. In the synagogue the next morning my friend sat dejected. His sukkah had blown down. "What happened to yours?" he asked. "It's still standing," I said. He could hardly believe it. His elaborate tabernacle had been overturned while my makeshift hut survived. "I must come round and see it," he said. "I don't understand how any sukkah could have stayed standing after that storm."

So we went to my home together to investigate the mystery. We soon found the answer. Unlike his, our sukkah did not stand alone. It had three walls, and for the fourth we had rested it against the house. To stop it collapsing, I had joined one corner to the wall of the house with a single nail, and it was that nail that had held firm through the gale.

My friend laughed and said, "Now I understand the meaning of Sukkot. You can plan and build the most sophisticated structure, but if it is not joined to something stable, one day the winds will come and blow it down. Or you can make an improvised shelter that looks frail, and probably is. But if it is joined, even at only one point, to something immovable, it will hold fast in the worst storm." Looking at the nail in the corner with a smile I have never forgotten, he said, "That nail is faith."

title: The Broken Glass and the Eternal Light
text:
A Rosh Yeshiva from Jerusalem went to Italy to open hearts and pockets. He entered the home of a wealthy Jew in Milan and stood stunned by the splendor before him. He had visited many rich homes, but he had never seen such good taste. Crystal chandeliers hung from the ceiling, the marble floor was covered with artistic rugs, and the living-room table was set with fine dishes.

Then he noticed a strange thing. In a glass cabinet stood a magnificent silver menorah, and beneath it lay a box of broken glass. How did broken glass fit with all this splendor? The man told him:

"I was born to a chassidic family. I studied in yeshiva and received a fine education. The whole family lived off the wealth of my grandfather, who ran a prosperous factory in Milan, and life was wonderful. One day a letter came from my grandfather. Old age was catching up with him, he wrote, and he asked me to come and help him in the business before it was too late. Our family lived off that business, so my parents had to take me out of yeshiva. I was drawn to running the factory, and I was very successful. Within two years I had stepped into my grandfather's shoes and grown the business. But little by little I forgot the education I had received.

"One day the time for a prayer passed and I had not walked to the synagogue; another time I fell asleep exhausted without saying the evening prayer; and one morning I did not find the time to take the tefillin out of their bag. Years passed. I looked for a wife who would match my social standing. She also came from a Jewish home, but she was not interested in tradition. That was the education we gave, or did not give, our children.

"One evening I was walking back from the office when I saw a group of Jewish children in the street. In the middle stood a boy in a yarmulke, sobbing: 'What will I tell Father? What will I explain to Father? Father will be so angry.' I asked the boy what had happened. He said that tonight was the first candle of Chanukah. His father had sent him to buy a bottle of olive oil. Hurrying home, he had dropped the bottle and it broke, and now he was frightened of his father's reaction. The father was a poor, downtrodden man, and the child was afraid he would be blamed. Of course I took out my wallet at once, gave him enough to buy another bottle of oil, and went home.

"I tried to go on with my routine, but the child's crying gave me no rest. 'What will I tell Father?' I am getting older too; soon my children will build their own homes. What will I say to my father, and to my Father in Heaven? Will generations of devotion to Jewish life stop and end because I was immersed in material success? The pain overtook me. For the first time in decades, I walked to the store and bought a bottle of olive oil to light Chanukah candles. I gathered the family, fried latkes, and told the story of the miracle.

"Then I did something else. I went back to the place where the children had been standing and swept up the broken glass from the ground. I wrapped the pieces in a newspaper and put them on my desk. Every day I remember how it all began. Every day I see with my own eyes that ugly, sharp, broken fragments can build an eternal light."

The Yom Kippur War left behind a fracture and a scar. So did every martyr, every broken soul, every shattered cruse of pure Chanukah oil. But we take that pain and with it we strengthen, and strengthen again, the building of our people. The Almighty will surely see our soul's devotion, our mesirat nefesh, in carrying on the existence of the people of Israel, and will open the Book of Life for us all with the complete and everlasting redemption.
source: Rabbi Paysach Krohn (heard from the Jerusalem maggid Rabbi Shabsai Yudelevitz), retold in 'Good Shabbos Everyone' (Breslev.com) and the Jewish Press ('A Chanukah Story', Torah Tavlin)

title: The Power of Care
text:
There was a boy named Gerald Wolpe who lived in Boston. When he was eleven his father suddenly died, and that changed every part of his life. His mother, a young widow, had to plunge at once into the working world to provide for herself and her young son. She became a waitress, with long, exhausting hours. Gerald missed his father day and night, but he had to hide his pain and tears for his mother's sake. She was carrying her own burdens, and he did not want to add to her grief by sharing his sense of loss.

Because of her hours, Gerald's mother was asleep when he began his day. Classes began at 8:30, but Gerald woke each morning at 5:30. It was a long walk to school, and on the way he stopped at the synagogue, which was halfway along his route. There, every morning, he joined the morning service to recite Kaddish, the mourner's prayer.

After the first week of this schedule, something unusual happened. The shamash of the synagogue began to appear at Gerald's front door just as he left for his walk to the synagogue. This was odd, because the shamash was not a young man, and during the previous week Gerald had noticed that he came to the minyan in a car driven by a congregant. Now, each morning, he seemed to be passing Gerald's home on foot just as Gerald set out for synagogue and school. The shamash explained, "Your home is on the way to the synagogue. I have to go this way, and I thought it might be fun to have some company. That way I don't have to walk alone."

Each morning he was there. They walked through the freeze of winter and the heat of summer. Each morning there was another story about the Jewish people, the prayer book, the questions of faith. The shamash listened to Gerald's grief and quietly reflected the tradition that deals with sorrow as it does with joy. He held Gerald's hand as they crossed busy intersections, and after some weeks he held Gerald's hand throughout the journey. Gerald sat next to him in the synagogue, and he listened, and he taught, and he hugged, and he moved into a void that was tearing at Gerald's heart and soul.

Years went by, and they kept in touch by phone and letters. The shamash was in his nineties. One day Gerald came back to visit Boston with his wife and young baby. He wanted the shamash to see his baby, so he phoned and asked him to come to the home he had passed so often. He agreed, but said it was impossible for him to walk; would Gerald please come to get him by car?

Gerald realized that he had never known where the shamash lived, so he asked for directions and set out. The journey was long and complicated. His home was far away. Gerald drove in tears as he understood what the shamash had done. Each morning, the shamash had walked many miles to Gerald's home so that the boy would not have to be alone. Gerald's home was not at all on the way to the synagogue; it was completely out of his way.

The shamash rose above his nature, like Abraham and Sarah. He had made Gerald feel that Gerald was helping him with companionship, when the opposite was true. The shamash knew the boy's loneliness, and he did not want Gerald's day to begin alone.

They met and embraced and wept. The shamash held Gerald's son. Members of the family stood by and watched; everyone wept. Each of them knew their story.
source: Rabbi David Wolpe (son of Rabbi Gerald Wolpe), as reported by San Diego Jewish World; Rabbi Gerald Wolpe of Boston (1927-2009) was a real rabbi (Har Zion, Philadelphia)

title: Viktor Frankl and the Shema
text:
When the Jewish psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was arrested by the Nazis in World War II, he was stripped of everything: property, family, possessions. He had spent years researching and writing a book on the importance of finding meaning in life, ideas that would later be known as logotherapy. When he arrived in Auschwitz, the infamous death camp, even his manuscript, which he carried in his coat pocket, was taken away.

"I had to undergo and overcome the loss of my spiritual child," Frankl wrote. "Now it seemed as if nothing and no one would survive me; neither a physical nor a spiritual child of my own! I found myself confronted with the question of whether under such circumstances my life was ultimately void of any meaning."

He was still wrestling with that question a few days later when the Nazis forced the prisoners to give up their clothes. "I had to surrender my clothes and in turn inherited the worn-out rags of an inmate who had been sent to the gas chamber," said Frankl. "Instead of the many pages of my manuscript, I found in the pocket of the newly acquired coat a single page torn out of a Hebrew prayer book, which contained the main Jewish prayer, Shema Yisrael" (Hear, O Israel, the L-rd our G-d, the L-rd is One. And you shall love the L-rd your G-d with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your might).

"How should I have interpreted such a 'coincidence' other than as a challenge to live my thoughts instead of merely putting them on paper?"

Later, reflecting on his ordeal in his book *Man's Search for Meaning*, Frankl wrote: "There is nothing in the world that would so effectively help one to survive even the worst conditions as the knowledge that there is a meaning in one's life... He who has a 'why' to live for can bear almost any 'how.'"
source: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (quoted on Chabad.org 'Shema Stories' and elsewhere)

title: The City Paid for It
text:
In Israel there is a legendary plumber, known for his golden hands and his golden heart. His wife convinced him that it was time to move out of their apartment and build a house with a garden, where the grandchildren could come over. He bought a plot of land, hired a contractor and compared bids for materials, but before he ordered anything he got a call: all the materials had already been delivered, by a building-supply company!

Angry, he went over to their office. There the owner told him a story.

Years ago there was a young widow with several children who had a terrible leak in her home. She called the plumber, who told her it was a big job: they would have to go into the walls, take walls down; it would be quite expensive. She said she would speak to her social worker and find out whether the city might pay for it. She went to the city, and they laughed at her. She was brokenhearted; the family's troubles were compounded by their leaking home, and they had no one to turn to.

Then one day she came home and found the plumber already halfway through the job. Walls were open, pipes were coming out and going in. The children stood watching the workers, as children do. Everything was done quickly and efficiently, sparkling new, even a fresh coat of paint on the walls. "What is this? How am I going to pay for it?" The plumber said, "Oh, it's paid for already. The city is paying for it." The kids, who were not so young, understood who "the city" was.

The owner turned to the plumber: "The widow was my mother. The kids watching you work were my brother and me. That's why I sent you the materials. It's paid for already. 'The city' paid for it."
source: The Jewish Press, 'On the Municipality's Account' (T. Gestetner, Lessons in Emunah column; 'names have been changed')

title: You Don't Have to Carry My Pack Too
text:
A farmer was driving along the road one scorching summer day when he came upon a small old peddler with a heavy load of merchandise on his back. The poor man looked utterly exhausted as he trudged along. The kindhearted farmer pulled his horse to a halt and offered the weary traveler a ride to the city.

They had been riding together for several minutes when the farmer noticed that his companion was still holding the heavy pack on his back. "My friend," he said, "why not set your pack down in the wagon and make yourself comfortable?"

"Sir, you are a kind man, and I don't want to take advantage of your goodness," answered the humble peddler. "It is enough that you are taking me to the city, and for that I thank you. But you don't have to carry my pack too!"
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: The Ice Cream Tip
text:
In the days when an ice cream sundae cost much less, a ten-year-old boy walked into a hotel coffee shop and sat down at a table. A waitress put a glass of water in front of him.

"How much is an ice cream sundae?" he asked.

"Fifty cents," replied the waitress. The little boy pulled his hand out of his pocket and studied the coins in it.

"How much is a dish of plain ice cream?" he asked.

By now people were waiting for a table, and the waitress was getting impatient. "Thirty-five cents," she said brusquely. The little boy counted the coins again. "I'll have the plain ice cream," he said.

The waitress brought the ice cream, put the bill on the table and walked away. The boy finished his ice cream, paid the cashier and left.

When the waitress came back, she began wiping down the table, and then she swallowed hard at what she saw. There, placed neatly beside the empty dish, were two nickels and five pennies: her tip.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: Shaya's Grand Slam
text:
At a fundraising dinner for Chush, a school in Brooklyn for Jewish children with learning disabilities, the father of a Chush child gave a speech that no one who heard it would ever forget.

After praising the school and its devoted staff, he cried out: "Where is the perfection in my son Shaya? Everything that G-d does is done with perfection. But my child cannot understand things as other children do. My child cannot remember facts and figures as other children do. Where is G-d's perfection?" The audience was shocked by the question, pained by the father's anguish, and stilled by his piercing words.

"I believe," the father answered, "that when G-d brings a child like this into the world, the perfection He seeks is in the way people react to this child." Then he told this story about his son.

Shaya attends Chush during the week and a boys' yeshiva on Sundays. One Sunday afternoon, Shaya and his father came to the yeshiva as his classmates were playing baseball. As they walked toward the field, Shaya asked, "Do you think you could get me into the game?" Shaya's father knew his son was not at all athletic, and that most boys would not want him on their team. But he also understood that if his son were chosen, it would give him a comforting sense of belonging. So he went up to one of the boys in the field and asked, "Do you think my Shaya could get into the game?"

The boy looked around for guidance from his teammates. Getting none, he took matters into his own hands: "We're losing by six runs and the game is already in the eighth inning. I guess he can be on our team, and we'll try to put him up to bat in the ninth." Shaya's father was ecstatic, and Shaya smiled broadly. Shaya was told to put on a glove and go out to short center field.

In the bottom of the eighth, Shaya's team scored a few runs but was still behind by three. In the bottom of the ninth they scored again, and now, with two outs and the bases loaded and the winning runs on base, Shaya was due up to bat. Would the team really let Shaya bat now and give away their chance to win? Surprisingly, Shaya was told to take a bat and try to get a hit. Everyone knew it was all but impossible; Shaya did not even know how to hold the bat properly, let alone hit with it.

As Shaya stepped up to the plate, the pitcher moved in a few steps to lob the ball softly, so that Shaya could at least make contact. The first pitch came in; Shaya swung clumsily and missed. One of his teammates came up, and together they held the bat and faced the pitcher. The pitcher took a few more steps forward and tossed the ball gently. Shaya and his teammate swung together and hit a slow ground ball to the pitcher. The pitcher picked up the soft grounder and could easily have thrown it to first base. Shaya would have been out, and the game would have been over.

Instead, the pitcher threw the ball in a high arc to right field, far beyond the first baseman's reach. Everyone started yelling, "Shaya, run to first! Shaya, run to first!" Never in his life had Shaya run to first. He scampered down the baseline, wide-eyed and startled. By the time he reached first, the right fielder had the ball. He could have thrown it to second to tag Shaya out, but he understood what the pitcher had intended, so he threw it high and far over the third baseman's head, as everyone yelled, "Shaya, run to second!" Shaya ran toward second as the runners ahead of him circled the bases toward home. As he reached second, the opposing shortstop ran over, turned him toward third and shouted, "Shaya, run to third!" As Shaya rounded third, the boys from both teams ran behind him screaming, "Shaya, run home! Shaya, run home!"

Shaya ran home, stepped on home plate, and all eighteen boys lifted him onto their shoulders and made him the hero: he had just hit the "grand slam" and won the game for his team.

"That day," said the father, with tears rolling down his face, "those eighteen boys reached their level of perfection. They showed that it is not only the talented who deserve to be recognized, but also those with less talent. They too are human beings; they too have feelings and emotions; they too are people; they too want to feel important."
source: Rabbi Paysach Krohn (ArtScroll Maggid series; told him by Shaya's father), as checked by TruthOrFiction.com ('God's Perfection')

title: Mathilde Rathenau's Letter
text:
The most powerful story about repentance I know concerns Ernst Werner Techow, one of three German right-wing terrorists who assassinated Walter Rathenau, Germany's Jewish foreign minister, in 1922. The killers were driven by political extremism and anti-Semitism.

When the police caught the assassins, two committed suicide; Techow alone survived. Three days later, Mathilde Rathenau, the victim's mother, wrote to Techow's mother: "In grief unspeakable, I give you my hand, you of all women the most pitiable. Say to your son that, in the name and spirit of him he has murdered, I forgive, even as G-d may forgive, if before an earthly judge your son makes a full and frank confession of his guilt, and before a heavenly judge repents. Had he known my son, the noblest man earth bore, he would have rather turned the weapon on himself. May these words give peace to your soul."

Techow was released from prison after about seven years.

Years later, Techow met a nephew of Rathenau and confided that his repentance and transformation had been set off by Mathilde Rathenau's letter. He said: "Just as Frau Rathenau conquered herself when she wrote that letter of pardon, I have tried to master myself. I only wished I would get an opportunity to right the wrong I have done."
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: Be a Player, Not a Fan
text:
It was a chilly winter night in 1955 when Rabbi Shimshon Stock ushered a close acquaintance and his soon-to-be bar mitzvah son into 770 Eastern Parkway, Lubavitch World Headquarters. They had come for a blessing from the Lubavitcher Rebbe. In those years, before a boy turned thirteen he would have a private audience, a yechidus, with the Rebbe to receive his blessing before the bar mitzvah. The Rebbe did not always engage the bar mitzvah boys in conversation, but there are countless stories of the Rebbe testing them on what they were learning.

The Rebbe briefly blessed the boy that he should grow up to be a source of pride to the Jewish people and to his family. And then the Rebbe surprised all three Americans in the room by asking the youngster, "Are you a baseball fan?"

The bar mitzvah boy replied that he was.

"Yankees or Dodgers?" The Dodgers, replied the boy.

"Does your father have the same feeling for the Dodgers as you have?" No.

"Does he take you to games?" Well, every once in a while his father took him to a game. They had been at a game a month ago.

"How was the game?" asked the Rebbe. It was disappointing, the thirteen-year-old confessed. By the sixth inning the Dodgers were losing nine to two, so they decided to leave.

"Did the players also leave the game when you left?"

"Rabbi," the boy exclaimed in surprise, "the players can't leave in the middle of the game!"

"Why not?" asked the Rebbe. "Explain to me how this works."

There are players and there are fans, the baseball fan explained. The fans can leave whenever they like; they are not part of the game, and the game can go on, and does, without them. But the players have to stay and try to win until the game is over.

The Rebbe smiled at the boy. "In the game of life," he explained, "there are two kinds of people. There are some who just watch from the stands, but they never become part of the game. This is the lesson I want you to take for life," said the Rebbe with a smile. "You can either be a fan or a player. Spend your life being a player."
source: Chabad.org, 'Fans and Players'; COLlive (Dovid Zaklikowski, Hasidic Archives)

title: Light Your Own Candle
text:
Mr. Yehudah Avner was an advisor to five Israeli Prime Ministers and later Israel's ambassador to Britain and Australia. In 1977 he met with President Carter, and then Menachem Begin sent him to report to the Rebbe. He sat with the Rebbe for several hours, and they discussed many subjects.

At midnight, the Rebbe saw that Yehudah Avner was tired. He put his holy hand on him and asked him why he was not a chassid. Mr. Avner replied that there were people in his family who saw powers in the Rebbe that the Rebbe himself did not even realize he had. The Rebbe then told Mr. Avner what his job entails: "You open a cupboard and see a candle inside. In reality it is not a candle. It is only a lump of wax with a string through the middle: the wax is the body, and the wick is the soul. When does it become a candle? Only when you put a flame to it. Then it becomes a candle and fulfills the purpose for which it was created." And the conversation moved straight on to the next subject.

In the small hours of the morning the meeting ended. As Mr. Avner rose to leave, he turned to the Rebbe and asked, "Has the Rebbe lit my candle?"

The Rebbe smiled and replied, "No. I have only given you the match. You need to light your own candle!"
source: Chabad.org / JEM 'Here's My Story', Ambassador Yehuda Avner, 'The String and the Flame'; Yehuda Avner, The Prime Ministers (2010)

title: The Neighbor's Laundry
text:
Newly married, David and Sarah moved into a neighborhood in Jerusalem, picturesque, but certainly different from what they were used to back in America. The next morning, while they were eating breakfast, Sarah saw her neighbor hanging her wash outside.

"That laundry is not very clean," she said. "She doesn't know how to wash properly. Perhaps she needs better laundry soap. Maybe I should say something to her." David said nothing.

Every time the neighbor hung out her wash, Sarah made the same remarks. About a month later, Sarah was surprised to see a nice clean wash on the line, and said to David, "Look, she has learned how to wash properly. I wonder who taught her?"

David said, "I got up early this morning and cleaned our windows."
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: The Cost of Lying
text:
A poor Jew found a wallet with $700 in it. At his synagogue he read a notice: a wealthy congregant had lost his wallet and was offering a $100 reward. He spotted the owner and handed him the wallet.

The rich man counted the money and said, "I see you already took your reward."

"What?" said the poor man.

"This wallet had $800 in it when I lost it."

They began to argue, and in the end they came before the rabbi. Each stated his case. The rich man finished by saying, "Rabbi, I trust you believe *me*."

"Of course," said the rabbi, and the rich man smiled. The poor man was crushed.

Then the rabbi handed the wallet to the poor man.

"What are you doing?!" yelled the rich man.

"You are, of course, an honest man," the rabbi answered, "and you say the wallet you lost had $800 in it. So I am sure it did. But if the man who found this wallet were a liar and a thief, he would not have returned it at all. Which means this wallet must belong to somebody else. If that person steps forward, he will get the money. Until then, it belongs to the man who found it."

"And what about my money?" asked the rich man.

"Well, we will just have to wait until somebody finds a wallet with $800 in it."
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: Don't Forget Us
text:
In a small village in the backwoods of Eastern Europe, many hours' journey from the nearest Jewish community, there lived a Jewish family. Once a year, for the holy day of Yom Kippur, they made the long trip to town to pray together with their fellow Jews.

One year the villager woke bright and early on the day before Yom Kippur and readied himself for the journey. His sons, not quite as industrious as he, had slept in. Impatient to get on his way, he told his family, "Listen, I'm going to set out on foot while you get yourselves together. I'll wait for you at the large oak at the crossroads."

Walking swiftly, the villager soon reached the tree and lay down in its shade to wait for the family wagon. Exhausted from several days of backbreaking labor, he fell asleep. Meanwhile his family loaded the wagon and set out. But in the excitement of the journey they forgot all about their old father and drove right past the sleeping figure at the crossroads.

When the villager woke, evening had already fallen. Many miles away, the Kol Nidrei prayers were getting underway in the town's synagogue. Lifting his eyes to the heavens, the old man cried: "Master of the Universe! My children have forgotten me. But they are my children, so I forgive them. You, too, should do the same for those of Your children who have abandoned You..."
source: MeaningfulLife.com (Rabbi Simon Jacobson), 'Yom Kippur Stories', excerpted from the book Inside Time (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: The Faith of the Jews
text:
On the eve of Passover, Reb Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev went out into the street of his town. He met the local smuggler and asked whether he could get him some contraband tobacco and embroidered brocades. The Polish-Russian border was closed, and smuggling was a capital offense. In less than an hour, the goods were in the Rebbe's hands.

The tzaddik then began walking the streets of Berditchev, knocking on doors. When the owner opened, the Rabbi asked him for a piece of pumpernickel bread. In every case the householder was shocked and dismayed that the Rebbe would accuse him of having chametz in the house. He calmed their worries and went on his way.

After several hours of this, Reb Levi Yitzchak went to the shul, threw open the doors of the holy ark and called out: "Master of the Universe! The borders are heavily guarded, and yet in less than an hour this contraband was in my hands. Your people, out of love for You, are embarrassed by the mere suggestion that they have chametz, and there are no guards at all. Who is like Your people Israel! The czar needs guards and police, and You need none."
source: Chabad.org, 'Minister for the Defense' (Rabbi Elisha Greenbaum) (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: The Cantonists' Ne'ilah
text:
Reb Mordechai, a chassid of the third Rebbe of Chabad, Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch (1789-1866), had been sent by his Rebbe to wander the Russian countryside, going from town to town to inspire the Jews scattered there with the teachings of Chassidism. One day, the day before Yom Kippur, he arrived in a town in the middle of nowhere, only to hear that all its Jews, about a hundred in all, had left the day before for the city of Vitebsk, to pray in the large synagogue there on the Day of Atonement.

Suddenly, a few hours before the holiest day of the year, he found himself without a minyan, the quorum of ten Jews needed for communal prayer. "You won't find any Jews here, Rabbi," one of the townspeople told him. "But about two hours away there's a small village of Cantonists. They're a strange bunch, but that's the closest thing to Jews you'll find around here now."

The Cantonists were Jews who, by decree of Czar Nicholas I, had been snatched from their families as young children for a 25-year term of "service" in the Czar's army, where every cruel means was used to force them to abandon Judaism. The few who survived came out decades later so broken in body and spirit that they could never live normal lives. So they lived together in little villages, apart from the rest of the world.

Reb Mordechai set out at once. After more than an hour he still saw nothing. Then, on the horizon, something appeared: a few old wooden houses. This must be the village. The first resident who saw the rabbi enter called the others, and in no time they were all lined up with shining faces, taking turns shaking the newcomer's hand. They were overjoyed. Such an honor, a real rabbi as their guest!

Then they stepped back, formed a sort of huddle and began whispering. They fell silent, looked at the rabbi again, and one of them stepped forward in great humility, cleared his throat and announced: "Excuse me, Rabbi, but we would be very honored if his excellency the Rabbi would honor us by leading the prayers of Yom Kippur." The others stood staring at him with wide, pleading eyes, nodding their heads. Reb Mordechai agreed, and the joyous handshaking began all over again. "We have only one condition," the man went on. "One of us leads Ne'ilah, the closing prayer of the holy day."

An hour later they were all seated in the solemn atmosphere of Yom Kippur in their little shul, listening to the beautiful, heartfelt prayers of the Chassidic rabbi. A very special feeling came over Reb Mordechai. He had never experienced a Yom Kippur like this. He had never been in such a minyan: Jews each of whom had been through hell, things he could never even dream of, only for the sake of G-d. He knew all the books and they knew nothing, yet he felt dwarfed by these simple folk.

His soul flowed into the prayers, and it seemed to him he had never sung so beautifully in his life. First Kol Nidrei, then the evening prayer; the following day he led the other three prayers and read twice from the Torah. Finally, at the end of the day, came their turn. It was time for Ne'ilah.

Reb Mordechai stepped back, took a seat with everyone else and waited to see what would happen. Why did they want this prayer for themselves? One of the Cantonists rose, took a few steps forward and stood at the podium, his back to the crowd. Then, before he began, he started unbuttoning his shirt and taking it off. Reb Mordechai was about to protest: you can't take your shirt off in the synagogue! But as the shirt fell from the man's shoulders, it revealed hundreds of scars, years upon years of deep scars, each one because the man had refused to forsake the G-d of Israel.

Reb Mordechai gasped, and tears ran down his face. The Cantonist raised his hands to G-d and said in a loud voice: "G-d, send us Moshiach! Redeem the Jewish people now! I'm not asking for the sake of our families, because we have no families. I'm not asking for the sake of our futures, because we have no futures. I'm not asking for the sake of our livelihoods, our comfort, our children or our reputations, because we have none of those things either. We are only asking: *Asei l'maan shemecha*, do it for Your sake!"

Then he put his shirt back on and began the prayer.
source: Chabad.org, 'The Cantonists' Minyan' (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: The Drought and the Missing Umbrellas
text:
The story is told of a community suffering from a severe drought. The elders proclaimed a day of prayer and fasting, in the hope of arousing G-d's compassion.

As they were about to enter the synagogue, a little girl turned to her father and said, "Daddy, you grown-ups don't really believe these prayers will help, do you?"

"Why do you say that?" asked the father.

"Well," said the little girl, "none of you brought umbrellas."
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: The Power of a Tallis
text:
We hold our Shabbos services in a hotel, so it is not surprising that people find us, whether they are staying at the hotel or looked us up on the web. A few months ago I was walking to our "davening room," our shul, when a heavyset Israeli came running up to me, gave me a warm "Shalom Aleichem," and blurted out: "You must be from Chabad! I was sitting in the restaurant at a business meeting and noticed you walk by. I didn't want to lose you, so I ran after you to tell you I'll be coming to shul. And I especially want to share an unbelievable but true story with you.

"During the Yom Kippur War, I was in charge of a group of soldiers. We had tanks and heavy artillery supporting us. Yet the first two days of the war were a sheer disaster. We were completely overrun by the Egyptians. There we were in enemy territory: most of our group killed, the tanks destroyed, our communications cut off, our radios dead, and we were worn down, exhausted and beaten.

"Suddenly, in the distance, we saw Israeli flags waving in the breeze, and a group of Israeli tanks. We were saved! Israeli reserves had been sent to rescue us! We sprang to our feet and, with all the energy we could muster, ran as fast as we could toward the rescue team. But the sight that met our eyes was devastating: they were taking aim at us. They had mistaken us for Arabs because of our unkempt, unshaven, filthy appearance after two days of heavy fighting.

"Without wasting a moment, one of my soldiers pulled a tallis from his pack and ran straight toward the tanks, through flying bullets, waving it high in the air. That heroic act identified us as Jews, and he saved us all.

"Where did that tallis come from? It was his own. When we retreated he had salvaged it, together with his tefillin, and carried it with him. At the time I didn't want to pray, I didn't believe. But now, every time I see a tallis, I remember that I am alive today because of one."
source: JTA (1998), 'Remembering Yom Kippur War: survivor of Egyptian onslaught recalls hellish days of October' (Yossi Harel, Milano post, Bar Lev line)

title: How Poor We Are
text:
One day the father of a very wealthy family took his son on a trip to the country, to show him just how poor some people are. They spent a couple of days on the farm of a very poor family.

On the way home, the father asked, "Son, how was the trip?"

"It was great, Dad."

"Did you see how poor people can be?"

"Oh yeah," said the son.

"So what did you learn?"

The son answered, "I learned that we don't allow pets in our fancy house, but they have dogs and cats they enjoy very much. We have a pool that reaches to the middle of our garden, and they have a creek that has no end. We have imported Japanese lanterns in our garden, and they have the stars at night. We have a small piece of land to live on, and they have fields that go beyond our sight. We have servants who serve us, but they serve others. We have walls around our property to protect us; they have friends to protect them."

The father was speechless. Then his son added, "Thanks, Dad, for showing me how poor we are."
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: The Captain Is My Father
text:
A boy was once playing by himself on the beach. A passerby stopped and asked why he didn't go and play with the other children at the far end of the beach.
