Bernie and Estelle had a big argument and stopped speaking. After three days, Bernie realized he needed Estelle's help: he had an early flight. Too proud to talk, he left a note on her pillow: "Please wake me at 5 a.m. I have to catch a plane."

He woke up to bright sunlight. It was 9 a.m., and the plane was long gone. Estelle was humming in the kitchen. On his own pillow lay a note: "It's 5 a.m. Wake up."

title: Miriam and the Batteries
text:
Moishe and Miriam were shopping. All Moishe wanted was a pack of batteries, but none of the clerks in the electronics store would help him.

"I have an idea," said Miriam. She took a tape measure from her purse and started measuring a giant flat-screen TV.

Faster than you can say "high definition," a young man came running. "May I help you?"

"Yes," said Miriam. "We'd like to buy these batteries."

title: The One-Handed Rabbi
text:
A man walks into a bar in Jerusalem and says to the bartender, "I'm looking for a rabbi."

"In Yerushalayim you can't find a rabbi?" says the bartender. "What kind do you want?"

"A one-handed rabbi."

"Why on earth a one-handed rabbi?"

"Because every time I ask a rabbi a question, he says, 'Well, on the one hand this, and on the other hand that.'"

title: A Great Marriage
text: At a party, the talk turned to marriage counseling. "Oh, we'll never need that," said one husband. "My wife and I have a wonderful relationship. She majored in communications, and I majored in theater. She communicates well, and I act like I'm listening."

title: The New Butler
text:
A Jewish couple won twenty million pounds in the lottery and moved into a grand house in Knightsbridge. They hired a very proper British butler. The next day they told him to set the dining table for four, because the Cohens were coming for lunch, and went shopping.

When they came home, the table was set for eight. "Why eight?" they asked. "We said four."

"Madam," said the butler, "the Cohens telephoned. They said they were bringing the blintzes and the knishes."

title: Moishe Cohen, the Perfect Man
text:
A man hailed a cab. "Perfect timing," said the driver. "You remind me of Moishe Cohen. That man did everything right. He could have been a tennis pro. He golfed with the pros. He sang like an opera star and danced like Broadway. He remembered everyone's birthday, knew wine, knew which fork to use, and could fix anything. Me? I change a fuse and the whole neighborhood goes dark."

"Sounds like quite a man. You knew him well?"

"Never met him," said the driver. "I married his widow."

title: Milk and Eggs
text:
A wife asked her husband, "Could you please go shopping and buy one carton of milk? And if they have eggs, get six."

A little later he came back with six cartons of milk.

"Why six cartons of milk?" she asked.

"They had eggs," he said.

title: The Back-Seat Cook
text:
A wife was frying eggs for breakfast when her husband burst into the kitchen. "Careful! Add more butter! You're cooking too many at once! Turn them! Turn them now! Don't forget the salt! THE SALT!"

She stared at him. "What in the world is wrong with you? You think I don't know how to fry a couple of eggs?"

"I just wanted to show you," he said calmly, "what it feels like when I'm driving."

title: Abe in the Waiting Room
text:
"Just relax," the hospital staff kept telling Abe, but it was no use. His wife was in labor, and he was a nervous wreck.

After what felt like a week, a nurse came out with the news. "It's a girl!"

"Thank G-d," said Abe. "She'll never have to go through what I just went through!"

title: Paul Asks for a Raise
text:
Paul went to see his boss. "My wife Natalie says I should come to you and ask for a raise. She says I'm entitled to one."

His boss replied, "Come back tomorrow. I'll ask my wife whether I should give it to you."

title: After Kol Nidrei
text:
The chazzan, the cantor, came home on Kol Nidrei night looking a bit down. His wife asked what was wrong.

"Schwartz, the shamash, told me I wasn't very good tonight."

"Schwartz?" said his wife. "Forget about him. He doesn't know anything. He just repeats what everyone else says."

title: The Bigger Steak
text:
One night at dinner the wife said, "When we were first married, you took the small piece of steak and gave me the bigger one. Now you take the big one and leave me the small one. You just don't love me anymore."

"Nonsense," said the husband. "You just cook better now."

title: The Producer and the Sermon
text:
A famous TV producer came to Rosh Hashanah services at a shul in Hollywood. The rabbi gave a forty-five-minute sermon on repentance and holiness.

Afterward, the producer introduced himself. "Rabbi, I produce a very successful news show. Could you condense your sermon into three minutes?"

The rabbi, already dreaming of national television, said, "Yes! I could do that."

"Nu," said the producer, "then why didn't you?"

title: Three Parrots in Bnei Brak
text:
A man strolling through Bnei Brak found a tiny shop with three parrots in the window. "How much for the one on the left?"

"Twenty-five thousand. This parrot knows Chumash with Rashi and a dozen other commentaries."

"And the middle one?" "Fifty thousand. He knows the whole Talmud, Bavli and Yerushalmi, with all the commentaries."

"And the one on top, a hundred thousand? What does he do?"

"I don't know," said the shopkeeper. "But the other two call him 'Rebbe.'"

title: The Accountant's First Worry
text:
A young man fresh out of business school interviewed with the nervous owner of a small company. "I need someone with an accounting degree," the man said, "but mostly I need someone to do my worrying about money."

"And what does the job pay?"

"I'll start you at eighty thousand."

"Eighty thousand! How can such a small business afford that?"

"That," said the owner, "is your first worry."

title: The Man in the Hospital Hallway
text:
A man was seen sprinting down the hospital corridor just before his operation. "What's the matter?" someone asked.

"I heard the nurse say, 'It's a very simple operation. Don't worry, I'm sure it will be all right.'"

"She was only trying to comfort you."

"She wasn't talking to me," he said. "She was talking to the doctor."

title: The Letter with One Word
text:
A rabbi was opening his mail one morning. One envelope held a single sheet of paper with a single word on it: "FOOL!"

The following Shabbat he told the congregation, "I have known people who write letters and forget to sign their names. But this week I received a letter from someone who signed his name and forgot to write the letter."

title: The Other Man's Invoice
text:
Hymie was in the dentist's chair, about to have extensive and expensive cosmetic work done. His dentist, Moshe, smiled. "Hymie, you're lucky you came to me. When I'm finished, you'll be another man entirely."

"I'm glad to hear that, Moshe," said Hymie. "So don't forget to send the invoice to this other man."

title: The Blind Man and the Matzah
text:
A blind man sat on a park bench. A rabbi sat down beside him, chomping on a piece of matzah. Feeling sorry for the man, the rabbi broke off a piece and handed it over.

A few minutes later the blind man tapped the rabbi on the shoulder. "Who wrote this rubbish?"

title: Chaim Yankel's First Hotel
text:
Chaim Yankel checked into a hotel for the first time in his life. Five minutes after going up to his room, he phoned the front desk. "You've given me a room with no exit. How do I get out?"

"Sir, that's absurd. Have you looked for the door?"

"Well, one door leads to the bathroom. Another goes into the closet. And there's a third I haven't tried, but it has a 'Do Not Disturb' sign on it."

title: Itzik and the Horn
text:
Rush hour in Tel Aviv, and Itzik's car died at a red light. The driver behind him leaned on his horn without stopping.

Finally Itzik got out, walked back to him and said with a smile, "I can't get my car started. Would you try it for me? I'll sit in your car and lean on your horn."

title: The Boss Calls
text:
My boss phoned me today. "Is everything okay at the office?"

"Yes, it's all under control. A very busy day. I haven't stopped for a minute."

"Can you do me a favor?"

"Of course. Anything."

"Hurry up and take your shot. I'm right behind you on the seventh hole."

title: The New Rabbi's Problem
text:
After a while, the new rabbi heard a rumor that people weren't happy. He asked the president of the shul, "What's the problem? Are my sermons boring?"

"No, very inspiring."

"Am I too strict?"

"No, just right."

"Then what is it?"

"Well, the old rabbi was with us a long time. He was elderly. It's not your fault."

"I promise you," said the rabbi, "I will work on growing older every day."

title: "I'm Not Free. I'm Four."
text:
The Fourth of July weekend was coming, so a nursery school teacher talked to her class about being grateful. "We live in a great country," she said. "One thing to be happy about is that here, we are all free."

A little boy came walking up from the back of the room, put his hands on his hips and announced, "I'm not free. I'm four."

title: Thirteen Rabbis in a Storm
text:
Thirteen rabbis were flying to Jerusalem when the plane hit a terrible thunderstorm. One of them called over the flight attendant. "Please tell the pilot not to worry. There are thirteen very religious people on this plane."

A few minutes later she came back from the cockpit. "The pilot says he's delighted to hear we have thirteen holy people aboard. But he'd still rather have one good engine."

title: The Pretzel Lady
text:
A little old lady sold pretzels on a street corner for a quarter each. Every day at lunchtime, a nice young man from the office building left her a quarter and never took a pretzel. For three years they never spoke.

One day, as he left his quarter as usual, she spoke up. "Sir, I appreciate your business. You're a good customer. But I have to tell you, the price has gone up to thirty-five cents."

title: The Rabbi at the Gas Station
text:
Just before a long holiday weekend, a rabbi waited in line at the gas station. The attendant worked fast, but there were many cars ahead of him. At last he waved the rabbi to a free pump.

"Rabbi, I'm so sorry for the delay," said the young man. "It seems like everyone waits until the last minute to get ready for a long trip."

The rabbi smiled. "I know what you mean. It's the same in my business."

title: Who Is Most Important?
text:
An architect, a surgeon and an economist were arguing about whose profession is the most important.

The surgeon said, "The very first thing G-d did was surgery: He took Eve from Adam's rib."

The architect said, "Wait. G-d was an architect first. He built the world in six days out of chaos."

The economist smiled. "And who do you think made the chaos?"

title: The Boy Who Never Spoke
text:
An eight-year-old boy had never said a word. One afternoon, over lunch, he turned to his mother and said, "The soup is cold."

His astonished mother cried, "You spoke! I waited so long to hear your voice. Why didn't you ever say anything before?"

The boy shrugged. "Up until now, everything was satisfactory."

title: My Mother's Bananas
text:
At a Tel Aviv hospital, a nurse asks each new patient about allergies and puts a special bracelet on their wrist so all the staff will know. When she asked one elderly woman, the woman said she couldn't eat bananas.

Later that day the woman's son Itzik stormed out of the ward. "Who is responsible for labeling my mother 'bananas'?"

title: Charlie in New York
text:
Charlie, visiting New York at the height of tourist season, went back to a kosher restaurant he had loved on an earlier trip. Finally he caught the eye of an overworked waiter. "You know, it's been over five years since I first came in here."

"Sorry, sir," said the waiter with true New York charm. "You'll have to wait your turn. I can only serve one table at a time."

title: Joseph Asks for the Car
text:
Joseph had just passed his driving test and asked his father about using the car. "Bring your grades up, study a little Torah, get a haircut, and we'll talk," said his father.

A month later Joseph asked again. "I'm proud of you," said his father. "Your grades are up and you've been studying. But you didn't get a haircut."

Joseph said, "Dad, Samson had long hair, Abraham had long hair, Noah had long hair, even Moses had long hair."

"Yes," said his father, "and they walked everywhere they went."

title: Moishe and the Long Line
text:
Moishe saw a long line and, without knowing what it was for, joined it. After a while he wondered, "What am I waiting for?" He asked the man in front of him, who said, "I don't know. I saw a line, so I got on." So did the next man, and the next.

Finally Moishe reached the man at the front. "What is this line for?"

"I bent down to tie my shoe," he said, "and when I stood up, there was a line behind me."

"So why are you still standing here?"

"Now that I'm first, you think I'm giving it up?"

title: Two Rabbis in a Kosher Deli
text:
Rabbi Bloom and Rabbi Levy sat in their local kosher deli and ordered two glasses of water. Then they pulled homemade sandwiches from their coat pockets and began to eat.

Moshe, the manager, came over. "I'll give each of you a snack on the house. But please, you can't eat your own sandwiches in here."

The two rabbis looked at each other with a twinkle. Without a word, they shrugged, swapped sandwiches, and went on eating.

title: Three Philosophers and a Train
text:
Three philosophers were so deep in conversation at the station, solving the world's problems, that they didn't notice the time. A whistle blew, doors slammed, and the train began to pull out. They ran. The youngest jumped aboard easily. The second, older and heavier, just made it. The third, oldest of all, didn't, and sat down on a bench looking miserable.

A railway worker said, "Don't be upset, sir. There's another train in half an hour."

The philosopher looked up. "You don't understand. I was the one who was supposed to catch the train. My friends only came to see me off."

title: Three Fathers in Jerusalem
text:
Three men were in the maternity waiting room at Hadassah Hospital. A doctor told the first, "Mazel tov! Your wife had quadruplets." The man said, "What a coincidence! I live in Kiryat Arba. Arba is four."

Another doctor told the second, "Mazel tov! Septuplets." "Unbelievable! I live in Be'er Sheva. Sheva is seven."

Then the third man fainted onto the floor. The doctors revived him. "Sir, what happened?"

He smiled weakly. "I live in Mea Shearim. The neighborhood of a hundred gates."

title: Today's Special
text:
David and Betty Goldstein were backpacking around Israel when they spotted a little roadside restaurant. The blackboard read, "Today's Special: Vegetable Soup, Chicken Schnitzel and Grilled Vegetables." They both ordered the special.

When the food came, David called over the waiter, fuming. "The soup has no vegetables! The vegetables aren't grilled, they're baked! And this isn't chicken schnitzel, it's meatballs!"

The waiter was unmoved. "Chabibi, you're absolutely right. That's what makes it so special."

title: We Share Everything
text:
An elderly couple shuffled into a fast-food restaurant and ordered one meal. The wife carefully cut the sandwich in two and began eating her half, while her husband sat and watched. A kind customer offered to buy them another meal. "No, thank you, we share everything." A second customer made the same offer and got the same answer.

Finally one bystander couldn't stand it. "If you share everything, why aren't you eating?"

"I'm waiting for the teeth," said the husband.

title: The Rabbi Who Forgot His Watch
text:
A rabbi was giving a speech and, as rabbis sometimes do, he went on and on, far past his time. At last he stopped, noticed, and apologized. "I'm sorry, I left my watch at home."

A voice called out from the crowd, "But Rabbi, there's a calendar right in front of you!"

title: The Red Light in Tel Aviv
text:
At a busy corner in Tel Aviv, an old man, a vacationing couple and a young yeshiva student were waiting for the light to change. Impatient, the young man dashed across against the traffic.

The old man shook his head and said to the couple, "Look at him. For centuries he's been waiting for Moshiach, but he can't wait for a traffic light."

title: The Second Notice
text:
Dave had just made Aliyah and was still learning how things work in Israel. One day a sternly worded "second notice" arrived from the Tax Authority: his taxes were overdue.

Dave hurried to the office, paid up, and apologized. "I must have missed the first notice."

The clerk smiled. "Oh, we don't send first notices here. We've found the second ones work much better."

title: Why the Children Came
text:
One Chanukah, a mother decided to stop nagging her children about thank-you notes. Sure enough, Grandma never heard a word about the generous checks she had given them.

The next year was different. Grandma told her friend proudly, "The children came over in person to thank me!"

"How wonderful! What changed?"

"Oh, that's easy," said Grandma. "This year I didn't sign the checks."

title: The Seat Facing Backward
text:
Yecker planned a train trip from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Weeks ahead he told the travel agent exactly where he wanted to sit, facing the direction the train would travel.

On the day, everything was perfect except that his seat faced backward. Furious, he phoned the agent from Jerusalem.

The agent apologized and asked, "Why didn't you ask the passenger across from you to switch?"

"I would have," said Yecker, "but the seat was empty."

title: The Patient Waiter
text:
A customer in a restaurant kept the waiter running. First he was too hot and wanted the air conditioning up, then too cold and wanted it down, and so on for half an hour.

The waiter stayed calm and smiling the whole time. Finally another diner asked, "Why don't you throw him out?"

"Oh, I don't mind," the waiter said cheerfully. "We don't even have an air conditioner."

title: Fiddle or Violin?
text:
My cousin Murray runs a pawnshop, so I asked him to appraise my grandfather's old violin.

"Old fiddles aren't worth much, I'm afraid," he said.

"What makes it a fiddle and not a violin?"

"If you're buying it from me, it's a violin. If I'm buying it from you, it's a fiddle."

title: Why Are We Here?
text:
A father and his fourteen-year-old son lay on the grass in the park, watching clouds drift by. "Dad," asked the boy, "why are we here?"

The father took a deep breath. "I think we're here to teach a kid to bunt, to wear a favorite old cap on a Saturday morning with nowhere to be. The meaning of life isn't worrying about what comes after, it's tasting the small moments that come before. Grown-ups chase the perfect house while happiness walks by on a bicycle. Does that answer your question?"

"Not really," said the boy. "I meant, why are we here when Mom told us to pick her up forty minutes ago?"

title: The Man Who Wrote the Letters
text:
My grandmother told me how she ended up marrying Grandpa. In her twenties, the man she was dating went off to the war. "We were in love," she said, "and wrote to each other every week. That's when I discovered how wonderful your grandfather was."

"So you married Grandpa when the soldier came home?"

"Oh, I didn't marry the man who wrote the letters," she said. "Grandpa was the mailman."

title: The Fly and the Pickle
text:
My three-year-old held out her hand and announced, "Look, Mommy, I killed a fly!"

She was eating a juicy pickle at the time, so I rushed her hands to the faucet and scrubbed them with soap. Then I sat her down to finish her pickle and asked, with a touch of awe, "How did you ever catch that fly all by yourself?"

Between bites she said, "I hit it with my pickle."

title: The Bridal Registry
text:
Jacob, 92, and Rebecca, 89, were about to be married in their Florida retirement community. Out for a stroll to talk over the plans, they stopped at a drugstore.

"Are you the owner?" Jacob asked the pharmacist. "We're getting married. Do you sell heart medication?"

"Of course."

"Circulation? Rheumatism? Memory pills? Vitamins, sleeping pills, Geritol?"

"Absolutely, the works."

"Wheelchairs and walkers?"

"All speeds and sizes."

"Wonderful," said Jacob. "We'd like to register here for our wedding gifts."

title: A Doctor of What?
text:
At her daughter's party, old Mrs. Cohen heard a guest called "doctor" and shyly approached. "Doctor, may I ask a question? Lately I have a funny pain right here, under the heart..."

The guest squirmed. "I'm so sorry, Mrs. Cohen, but I'm a doctor of philosophy."

"Oh, forgive me!" She turned away, but curiosity won. She turned back. "Just one more question, doctor. What kind of disease is philosophy?"

title: The Absentminded Professor
text:
Professor Johnson's family was moving, and his wife, knowing how forgetful he was, tucked a slip of paper with the new address into each of his pockets.

But during the day he used every slip for notes and handed them out to his students. That evening he got in the car and suddenly remembered it was moving day. He had no idea where to go.

So he drove to the old house, where a little girl was playing outside. "Hi, sweetie," he said. "Can you tell me where the Johnsons moved to?"

"Sure," she said. "It's just around the corner and two doors down, Daddy."

title: The Family Vase
text:
A mother was working in the kitchen when her six-year-old called out, "Mommy! You know that beautiful vase in the dining room, the one handed down from generation to generation?"

"Yes," she said. "What about it?"

"Well," said the boy, "the last generation just dropped it."

title: Rabbi Bloom and the Doorbell
text:
Rabbi Bloom saw a very small boy trying to reach a doorbell that was far too high for him. "Would you like some help?" he called. "NO!" said the boy.

Still, the rabbi crossed the street, put a kind hand on the boy's shoulder, leaned over, and gave the bell a good, solid ring. Then he crouched down with a warm smile. "Is there anything else I can help you with, my little friend?"

"Yes," said the boy. "Run like mad!"

title: Don't Make the Rabbi Lose His Place
text:
After Shabbat services at a synagogue in Owensboro, Kentucky, a mother told her rabbi how she got her fidgety seven-year-old to sit still during the sermon.

Halfway through, she leaned over and whispered, "If you don't be quiet, Rabbi Cohen is going to lose his place and have to start the whole sermon over again!"

It worked beautifully.

title: A Middle Name for the Check
text:
Samuel Cohen, the oldest of seven, left school early to help support his family, and never learned to read. When he opened a bank account he simply signed his checks "XX." Years later his tailoring business in London flourished and he grew very wealthy.

One Thursday the bank called. "Mr. Cohen, for years you've signed "XX." This check has three X's. We wanted to be sure it's really yours."

Samuel sighed. "Since I became rich, my wife thought I should have a middle name."

title: Five Years of Imagination
text:
Several weeks after a young man was hired, the personnel manager called him in. "What is the meaning of this? You told us you had five years of experience, and now we find this is your very first job."

"Well," said the young man, "your ad said you wanted someone with imagination."

title: Salt Herring on Yom Kippur
text:
On Yom Kippur, between Musaf and Mincha, young Greg Shapiro approached his father's rabbi. "Rabbi Pollak, I know we're fasting, but I'm so thirsty. Please let me have something to drink!"

"I'm sorry," said the rabbi gently but firmly, "only when it's truly dangerous may the fast be broken."

Greg kept pleading that he was about to faint, until the rabbi gave in and had the gabbai, who handles the synagogue's honors, bring a small glass of water. Greg gulped it down and gasped, "That's the last time I eat salt herring for breakfast on Yom Kippur!"

title: Holmes and the Missing Tent
text:
Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson were camping. In the middle of the night Holmes woke his friend. "Watson, look up. What do you see?"

"Millions of stars."

"And what does that tell you?"

"That it's about two in the morning, by the stars. That it's the 15th of the month, by the moon..."

"Watson," said Holmes, "it tells us someone has stolen our tent."

title: The Wedding Dress
text:
Shoshana and David Epstein were about to be married, and Shoshana asked David's mother, Esther, if she might wear Esther's wedding gown. When she tried it on for the first time, she walked down the stairs to show her future mother-in-law. It fit her petite frame perfectly, and Esther's eyes filled with tears.

"You're not losing a son," Shoshana said softly. "You're gaining a daughter."

"Oh, forget that!" Esther sobbed. "I used to fit into that dress!"

title: The Cure for a Fear
text:
Simon was terrified that someone was hiding under his bed every night. He went to Dr. Bloom, a famous psychiatrist, who said, "I can cure you, but it takes twice a week for three years, at $515 a session, a special price for a friend."

"Oy, Doctor, that's too much for me," said Simon.

Months later they met in a supermarket. "Why didn't you come to me?" asked the doctor.

"Then my rabbi cured me for free," Simon said. "I was so happy about the savings that I took a month's vacation in Tel Aviv."

"And how did the rabbi cure you?"

"Easy. He told me to cut the legs off my bed."

title: What's for Dinner, Chana?
text:
Solly and Raziel invited their rabbi for dinner. While they cooked in the kitchen, the rabbi chatted with their five-year-old, Chana.

"Tell me, Chana, do you know what we're having tonight?"

"Goat," said Chana.

"Goat? Are you sure?"

"Oh yes, Rabbi. I heard Daddy tell Mommy, 'Today is as good a day as any to have the old goat for dinner.'"

title: Why Jay Was Sad
text:
The teacher noticed Jay looked down. "What's wrong, Jay?"

"My mom is at the hospital and my dad is at the police station."

"Oh, I'm so sorry, dear. Would you like to go home?" Jay said yes and left.

The teacher turned to the class. "Why is Jay's father at the police station and his mother at the hospital?"

"Because his dad is a policeman," said a classmate, "and his mom is a nurse."

title: Sent a Professional
text:
A woman got a call at work that her little daughter was sick with a fever. She stopped at the pharmacy for medicine, then came out to her car and found she had locked her keys inside. She bowed her head and asked G-d to send help.

Within minutes a bearded man in an old bandana pulled up on a battered motorcycle and offered to help. In no time the car was open. She hugged him, tears in her eyes. "Thank you, you're such a nice man!"

"Lady, I'm not a nice man," he said. "I just got out of prison yesterday. Car theft."

She hugged him again and cried out, "Thank you, G-d! You even sent me a professional!"

title: Excused From Jury Duty
text:
A man was trying hard to be excused from jury duty, to the judge's irritation.

"Tell me," the judge snapped, "is there any good reason you can't serve?"

"I don't want to be away from my job that long."

"Can't they do without you at work?"

"Yes," the man admitted. "But I don't want them to realize it."

title: So Much Nachas
text:
Two women who hadn't seen each other in years met on the street.

"How's your daughter, the one who married the surgeon?"

"They divorced."

"Oh, I'm so sorry."

"But then she married a lawyer."

"Mazal tov!"

"They divorced too. But now everything's fine. She married a very successful accountant."

The first woman shook her head. "Mmm, so much nachas, joy from children, from one daughter..."

title: Darling, Petal, Sweetheart
text:
Daniel and Rivkah celebrated their 50th anniversary with a dinner at their son Aaron's house. All evening Aaron was moved to hear his father call his mother "darling," "petal," and "sweetheart."

When Rivkah stepped out, Aaron kissed his father. "Dad, it's wonderful that after fifty years you still call Mom by those sweet names."

Daniel looked embarrassed. "Things aren't always what they seem, son. The truth is, I forgot your mother's name two years ago."

title: Is Israel a Healthy Place?
text:
Abe visited Israel for the first time. His taxi driver was friendly and full of tips, so Abe asked, "Is Israel a healthy place?"

"Oh, very," said the driver. "When I first came here, I couldn't say a single word, I had hardly any hair, I had no energy to cross a room, and every day I needed help getting out of bed."

"That's amazing!" said Abe. "How long have you been here?"

"I was born here."

title: Who Was Mr. Mann?
text:
An American tourist stood outside the Mann Auditorium in Tel Aviv, about to hear the Israel Philharmonic, admiring the sweeping entrance. "Is it named for Thomas Mann, the famous author?" he asked his friend.

"No, it's named for Frederic Mann of Philadelphia."

"Never heard of him. What did he write?"

"A check."

title: The Sleeping Pills
text:
Exhausted Chaim Yankel dragged himself into Dr. Shpielman's office. "Doctor, dogs bark all over my neighborhood day and night, and I can't get a wink of sleep!"

"Good news," said the doctor, rummaging in a drawer. "New sleeping pills, strong as a dream."

A few weeks later Chaim Yankel returned looking worse than ever. "Doctor, your plan is no good. I'm more tired than before!"

"Impossible! Those are the strongest pills on the market."

"Maybe," Chaim Yankel said wearily, "but I'm still up all night chasing the dogs. And when I finally catch one, it's hard to get him to swallow the pill!"

title: The Actor in the Ape Suit
text:
Dov, a down-and-out Jewish actor, answered an ad: "Actor needed to play ape." It turned out the zoo had overspent on renovations and couldn't afford a new ape, so until they could, Dov would wear an ape suit.

At first he felt silly, but soon he loved the attention and put on a show, swinging from vines and beating his chest. One day his hand slipped and he flew over the fence into the lion's den.

Terrified, Dov covered his eyes and cried out, "Shema Yisrael, Hashem Elokeinu, Hashem Echad!"

The lion opened its jaws and roared, "Baruch shem kevod malchuto l'olam va'ed!"

"Quiet, you two!" hissed a panda from the next cage. "You'll get us all fired!"

title: The Sleeping Congregant
text:
Every rabbi has at least one, a congregant who falls asleep during the sermon every single week. One rabbi had a long-running contest with his, and the congregant usually won.

One Shabbat, irritated by the man's look of blissful contentment, the rabbi raised his voice. "All who want to go to hell, stand up now!"

Jolted awake, the good-hearted fellow heard an appeal and rose to his feet. He looked around and said, "I don't know what you're asking for, Rabbi, but it looks like you and I are the only ones voting yes."

title: Facebook Without the Internet
text:
For those of us who cannot comprehend Facebook, I'm trying to make friends the same way, only offline. Every day I walk down the street and tell passers-by what I ate, how I feel, what I did last night, and what I'll do later. I hand out photos of my family and my cat, and selfies of me in front of landmarks. I listen to their conversations, give them a thumbs-up, and tell them I "like" them.

It works just like Facebook! I already have four followers: two police officers, a private investigator, and a psychiatrist.

title: Play Something by Request
text:
Itzik's Bistro in Tel Aviv was packed, as usual on open mic night. A band was playing while Shuki and his friend Dudu sat near the stage, not at all happy.

Finally Shuki called out to the bandleader, "Hey, can you play something by request?"

The bandleader beamed. "Of course! Whatever you like."

"Then sit down and play a game of shesh besh, backgammon," said Shuki, "so I can finish my meal."

title: A Walking Economy
text:
Izzy was strolling down Wall Street with his friend Jacob when he said, "Did you know I'm a walking economy?"

"What do you mean?"

"Well, my hairline is in recession, my stomach is a victim of inflation, and together they're putting me into a deep depression."

title: What If They Escape?
text:
Moishie and Shloimie, best friends, were talking at recess.

"I'm really worried," said Shloimie. "My dad works twelve hours a day to give me a nice home and good food. My mom spends all day cleaning and cooking for me. I'm worried sick!"

"What's there to worry about?" said Moishie. "Sounds like you've got it made!"

"What if they try to escape?"

title: Life Is Like a Cup of Tea
text:
Moskowitz and Finkelstein sat in a cafeteria with their tea. Moskowitz studied his cup and sighed. "Ah, my friend, life is like a cup of tea."

Finkelstein thought it over. "But why is life like a cup of tea?"

"How should I know?" said Moskowitz. "Am I a philosopher?"

title: How Soon Do You Need to Know?
text:
Rose and Sadie had been friends for over fifty years, and now their activities were down to a card game twice a week. As Rose dealt, Sadie said, "Now don't get mad at me. We've been friends so long, but I can't think of your name. I've tried for five minutes. Please, tell me your name."

Rose stared at her for a long moment. "How soon do you need to know?"

title: Telling Time With a Shofar
text:
Two old friends met after years apart and went back to one's house to catch up. After a while the guest said, "It's getting late. What time is it? I should be going."

"Hang on a minute," said his friend. He went to the cupboard and took out a shofar, the ram's horn we blow on Rosh Hashanah.

"What are you doing?"

"Telling the time," he said, and blew a loud blast.

From next door came a shout: "Are you crazy? It's one in the morning!"

title: The Special Golf Ball
text:
Two friends were about to tee off when one noticed that the other had only one golf ball. "Don't you have a spare? What if you lose it?"

"It's a special ball. I won't lose it."

"What if it goes in the lake?"

"It floats."

"What if it gets lost in the trees?"

"It has a homing beacon."

"What if we play till dark and you hit it into a sand trap?"

"It glows in the dark."

Finally satisfied, the friend asked, "Where did you get a ball like that?"

"I found it."

title: The Post-Dated Check
text:
A driver on a Texas road hit and killed a calf that had wandered across it. He went to the rancher, explained what had happened, and asked what the animal was worth.

"About $200 today," said the rancher. "But in six years it would have been worth $900. So I'm out $900."

The driver sat down, wrote a check for $900, and handed it over. "Here you are. It's post-dated six years from today."

title: The Laziest Man
text:
A site foreman had ten very lazy workers, so one day he tried a trick. "I've got an easy job today for the laziest one among you. Will the laziest man please raise his hand?"

Nine hands went up.

"Why didn't you raise yours?" he asked the tenth.

"Too much trouble," came the reply.

title: The Three-Thousand-Year-Old Mummy
text:
An archaeologist in the Israeli desert found a casket holding a mummy. "I've just found a 3,000-year-old mummy of a man who died of heart failure!" he announced. Tests confirmed it.

"How did you know it was heart failure?" asked a journalist.

"Simple. In his hand was a slip of paper that said, '10,000 shekels on Goliath.'"

title: Not “Just As”: A Father’s Shout in Riga
text:
In 1970, Rabbi Shlomo Riskin, then the rabbi of Lincoln Square Synagogue in New York, traveled to Riga, Latvia, on a mission for the Lubavitcher Rebbe: to help Jewish schools survive underground.

One night, around two in the morning, the gabbai (the man who runs a shul’s daily affairs) knocked at his door with a stranger. The man’s older son was nearing bar mitzvah age, and his newborn son was two weeks old. Neither boy had been circumcised. Under Soviet rule, that was dangerous. A Jewish doctor was willing to do it, but he needed a rabbi nearby to guide him.

The only safe place and hour was the Jewish cemetery outside the city, before dawn. Rabbi Riskin went.

Both brises were done quickly and well. Then Rabbi Riskin said the traditional closing line, which means: “Just as this child entered the covenant, so may he enter Torah, marriage and good deeds.” In Hebrew, the word for “just as” is *keshem*.

Suddenly the father cried out, “No! Not just as! I am not even religious. I only know I want my sons to be Jewish. But I don’t want their bar mitzvah and their wedding to be like this, hiding in a cemetery, afraid. I want them in the open, with joy, in Israel!”

Years later, that man’s grandson had his brit in Israel, openly and joyfully, and Rabbi Riskin was there to celebrate.

The Jewish spark can stay hidden for decades, and still burst out when it is needed.
source: Rabbi Shlomo Riskin, Listening to God: Inspirational Stories for My Grandchildren

title: What the Congregant Remembered
text:
A rabbi spent days preparing his Kol Nidre sermon. He delivered it to a packed shul and felt it was the best he had ever given.

A few days later, at the supermarket checkout, he overheard one of his congregants chatting with a friend from another shul. “So, what did your rabbi speak about on Yom Kippur?” the friend asked.

“Oh,” said the congregant, “about twenty minutes.”

title: The Cantor Who Sang Al Chet Gladly
text:
One Erev Yom Kippur, the Baal Shem Tov, founder of the Chassidic movement, arrived in a small village. The villagers were delighted to host him, and he asked who led the prayers.

He learned that the cantor sang the Al Chet, the long confession of sins, to a lively, cheerful tune. People found it odd. The Baal Shem Tov asked the cantor why.

The cantor answered with a parable. “Imagine a servant whose job is to clean the courtyard of the king’s palace. It is dirty work. But he loves the king, and he knows the king will be pleased to see the courtyard clean. So he sings as he works.”

“That is how I feel,” he said. “On Yom Kippur we clear away what we did wrong, and we do it for the King of Kings, who loves us and wants us close. Why shouldn’t I sing?”

The Baal Shem Tov was moved, and he chose to pray with that congregation.

The tale teaches that teshuvah, returning to G-d, is not only about sorrow. Cleaning house for someone you love can be done with a song.
source: A Chassidic tale, retold by Sivan Rahav-Meir

title: The Coal That Left the Fire
text:
There was once a man named Avraham who always came to shul, prayed with the minyan, joined the Torah classes and helped wherever he was needed.

Then one day he stopped coming. He felt he had outgrown the crowd and wanted to grow on his own, with a book, at home.

The rabbi came to visit. He found Avraham sitting by the fireplace and said nothing. He took a pair of tongs, lifted a single glowing coal out of the fire, and set it alone on the hearth.

The other coals kept burning brightly. The lonely coal flickered, dimmed and went out.

The rabbi nodded goodbye and left.

Avraham understood. The next Shabbat, he was back in shul.

Personal growth matters. But a flame burns brightest alongside others, and together we keep each other warm.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: Why We Step Aside at the Door
text:
In one shul, everyone entered in exactly the same way. They climbed the front steps, bowed, took three steps to the left, then three steps forward, bowed again, took three steps to the right, and only then went inside.

Year after year, everyone did it.

A new member finally asked why. “That is simply the proper way to enter a shul,” he was told. He was not convinced, so he went to the oldest member and asked him.

The old man smiled. “Many years ago, the shul was being renovated. Scaffolding blocked the front door, and to get in you had to duck under a plank and sidestep left and right. Like most renovations, it took forever. By the time the scaffolding came down, the ducking and sidestepping had become our minhag, our custom.”

It is a gentle reminder to ask, once in a while, why we do what we do. Some customs carry deep meaning. Others are just old scaffolding.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Rebbe and the Revolver
text:
In the summer of 1920, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, the sixth Rebbe of Chabad, was summoned in the middle of his morning prayers to the secret police in Rostov, in the Soviet Union. Soldiers marched him into a room where officials sat around a long table, a pistol lying in front of each. They were investigating religion, and they wanted him to give up his teaching.

The Rebbe answered that he would not give up his principles.

One of the officials lifted his pistol and said, “This little toy has made many people drop their principles.”

The Rebbe replied calmly that the toy might impress someone who has only one world and many gods. “But I have one G-d and two worlds,” he said. “It does not frighten me.”

The Rebbe was not harmed that day, and he kept building Jewish life in the Soviet Union, quietly and at great risk. The regime that threatened him is long gone, and Chabad communities now fill the region.

Fear of powerful people can shrink a life. A deep sense of what matters most can make us braver than we knew.

title: The Honest Prisoner
text:
The story goes that Frederick II, the eighteenth-century King of Prussia, once visited a prison in Berlin and spoke with the inmates.

One after another, the prisoners fell to their knees, wept about their fate and swore they were innocent.

Only one man stayed quiet. The king grew curious. “You there,” he said. “Why are you here?”

“Armed robbery, Your Majesty.”

“And are you guilty?”

“Completely, Your Majesty. I deserve my punishment.”

The king rapped his cane on the floor. “Warden! Release this guilty man at once. I won’t have him here, corrupting all these fine innocent people!”

Whatever its history, the tale points to something true about teshuvah, returning to G-d. It begins when we stop making excuses and say plainly, “I was wrong.” That honesty is where freedom starts.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Shofar on the Stormy Sea
text:
As Rosh Hashanah approached, a great and saintly rabbi, traditionally said to be Rabbi Elazar Rokeach of Amsterdam, was traveling by ship with his disciples. No land was in sight, so they prepared to spend the holiday at sea.

On the first night, a fierce storm struck. Huge waves crashed over the deck, and the sailors bailed until they were exhausted. The ship seemed about to sink.

The rabbi, in his cabin, was so absorbed in prayer that he did not notice a thing. At dawn his disciples came to his door twice, but were afraid to interrupt him. At last, when the storm was at its worst, they told him in tears that they were about to drown.

The rabbi asked them to bring his shofar. “Let us do the mitzvah while we are still alive,” he said.

He blew, and the sound seemed to be carried off by the wind. Then the wind died down, the sea grew calm, and the last note rang out in stillness.

The captain, certain the shofar was magic, offered to buy it. The rabbi smiled. It was an ordinary ram’s horn. He had not expected it to save them. He had simply wanted to do one more mitzvah. G-d had been kind, and now they should be grateful and keep His commandments always.

title: The Real Minister of Defense
text:
Margaret Thatcher, long before she became Prime Minister of Britain, served as Secretary of State for Education. Around then she met Immanuel Jakobovits, Britain’s Chief Rabbi, and the two became friends.

The Chief Rabbi told her something she never forgot: in truth, she was the nation’s Minister of Defense. What children learn at home and in school, he explained, is what keeps a people whole and strong. Education is the real defense.

Thatcher treasured the remark. Years later, at a dinner honoring the retiring Chief Rabbi, she recalled it with fondness, and she often spoke of how much he had taught her about Jewish education and Jewish schools.

Jewish tradition has always held the same view. Our children’s lessons at the family table, in the classroom and in the Torah they learn are what carry a people through every challenge.

title: Come Back Next Year
text:
A man was hunting for a pair of jeans at a garage sale. The seller had several pairs of Levi’s, in sizes 36, 38 and 40. But he needed a 42.

“Do you have any 42s?” he asked.

The owner shook his head. “I’m still wearing the 42s. Come back next year.”

Someone once said that our mistakes are a bit like that. Last year they were a 38, this year they’ve grown to a 40. This Rosh Hashanah is a good time to stop the growth before we reach 42.

title: The Violinist in the Subway
text:
On a cold January morning in 2007, a man in jeans and a baseball cap stood against a wall in a Washington, DC, metro station and began to play the violin. For about forty-five minutes he played six pieces by Bach while the rush-hour crowd streamed past.

The Washington Post had set it up as an experiment. Would people notice beauty in an ordinary place, at an inconvenient hour?

About a thousand people walked by. Almost none turned their heads. A few tossed in a dollar without breaking stride. Some children tried to stop and stare, and their parents tugged them along. Only seven people paused for even a minute. When the last note faded, nobody clapped. The violinist collected about thirty-two dollars.

He was Joshua Bell, one of the finest violinists in the world, playing an instrument worth millions. Just days earlier he had filled a concert hall in Boston, where good seats cost around a hundred dollars.

The story makes us wonder what else we hurry past. Jewish tradition answers with a gentle habit: we say blessings all day long, over bread, over a rainbow, over good news, simply to make ourselves stop and notice. Even a hundred blessings a day, the Sages say, is not too many.
source: The Washington Post, "Pearls Before Breakfast" by Gene Weingarten

title: "I Will Be Her Lungs"
text:
A man who had lost both legs to a land mine in Vietnam was working in his garage on a hot summer day when he heard a woman screaming from the house next door.

He rolled toward the sound in his wheelchair, but thick bushes blocked the way. So he climbed out and dragged himself through the dirt, whatever the pain. "I had to get there," he said later.

In the backyard, a little girl lay at the bottom of the pool. She had been born without arms and could not swim. He pulled her out. She was not breathing and had no pulse. While her mother called for help, he began CPR.

"Don't worry," he told the frantic mother. "I was her arms to get out of the pool. Now I am her lungs. Together we will make it."

Seconds later the girl coughed and began to cry.

The mother asked how he could be so sure. He answered that he wasn't. But years before, wounded and alone in a field, a village girl had dragged him to safety, whispering, "It's okay. You can live. I will be your legs." Those words had given him hope, and he wanted to give the same hope to someone else.

There are moments when none of us can stand alone, and when a kind word and a pair of willing hands are everything.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: Every Word Is Like Big Ben
text:
During World War Two, the BBC broadcast news to people living under Nazi occupation. Each program opened with the chimes of Big Ben, live from London, a sound that meant freedom to millions of listeners.

The story goes that this sound carried a hidden danger. German scientists, so it is told, noticed that the tone of the chimes changed slightly with London's weather, and passed that information to the bombers. When British intelligence found out, they replaced the live chimes with a recording.

Historians say the weather detail is probably a legend. What is true is that in 1944 the BBC did swap the live Big Ben for a recording, so that the enemy could not use the broadcast to learn what was happening over London. Even a single chime, it seems, can carry more than we realize.

That is the lesson of the tale. Our words are like those chimes. We say something in ten seconds, and ten years later it may still be heard, as a wound or as a gift, by people far from where we spoke.

That is why the Amidah, the central silent prayer, begins with a request: "G-d, open my lips, and my mouth will declare Your praise." We ask for help even to speak well.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Tootsie Roll Marines
text:
In late 1950, during the Korean War, thousands of American Marines found themselves surrounded by far larger forces near the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea. Temperatures fell to well below zero at night. Food froze, engines failed, and supplies had to be dropped by parachute.

The story is told that the Marines radioed their requests in code, in case the enemy was listening. "Tootsie Rolls" meant mortar shells. But the man at the other end, so they say, never got the code sheet, and took the request literally. Days later, crates of Tootsie Roll candy floated down from the sky.

To everyone's surprise, the candy turned out to be a gift. It thawed quickly, fit in a pocket, gave quick energy and lifted spirits. Some Marines even softened it over a flame to patch holes in their vehicles. The men broke out of the trap, and for years afterward veterans gathered and passed around Tootsie Rolls in memory.

A historian has questioned whether the airdrop really happened that way, and says candy was simply common in Marine supplies. That is why we tell it as a well-known tale, not a proven event.

Chassidic teaching has a name for events that look like mistakes but turn out to be exactly what was needed: Hashgachah Pratis, G-d's personal guidance in the details of our lives.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: Brandeis and the Professor
text:
A well-known story is told about Louis Brandeis, the brilliant Jewish lawyer who later became a justice of the United States Supreme Court. As a law student at Harvard, so the story goes, he faced a professor named Peters who looked down on him because he was Jewish.

One day Peters sat eating lunch when Brandeis sat down beside him with his tray. "Mr. Brandeis," sneered the professor, "a pig and a bird do not sit together to eat."

"Don't worry, professor," Brandeis replied calmly. "I'll fly away." And he moved to another table.

Furious, Peters tried again on an exam. "If you found two bags in the street, one full of wisdom and one full of money, which would you take?"

"The money, of course," said Brandeis.

"Just like a Jew," the professor smirked. "I would have taken the wisdom."

"Each of us takes what he lacks," said Brandeis with a shrug.

In the end, the professor scribbled one word, "idiot," across Brandeis's exam paper and handed it back. Brandeis stood up, walked to the front and said politely, "Professor, you signed my paper, but you forgot to give me a grade."

This tale circulates as true, but it is not found in any biography of Brandeis, and we cannot confirm it happened. We keep it as a parable about dignity and quick wit in the face of prejudice.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The King and the Butterfly
text:
Once there was a king who could read minds, and he was very proud of it. Every week he gathered his subjects and showed off his gift.

One day he noticed an old man in ragged clothes at the back of the hall. "I also read minds," the old man said when he was brought forward. "But my gift is from G-d, and I don't boast of it."

The angry king went behind a curtain and returned with a closed fist. "What is in my hand?" "A stone," said the old man. "A precious one. A tiny diamond." It was true.

The king tried again, with a single grain from a bowl of sugar. The old man named it at once. The crowd began to murmur that the king had met his match.

So the king planned a trap. He caught a butterfly and closed it in his hand. "Is it alive or dead?" If the old man said alive, the king would crush it. If he said dead, the king would open his hand and let it fly.

The old man looked deep into the king's eyes. "It is in your hands, King," he said. "Whether it lives or dies is up to you."

The same is true of us. Our words, our time and our kindness are in our hands, and what happens next is our choice.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: One Percent Better Every Day
text:
Every January, gyms fill up with people full of New Year's resolutions. By March, many of those people have disappeared. Big promises are hard to keep. Is there a better way?

Consider the British cycling team. For about a hundred years, British riders had hardly won anything at the top level. In 2003, the team hired a new performance director, Dave Brailsford, who tried a different idea: "marginal gains." Don't look for one huge change. Improve everything by a tiny amount.

So the team redesigned bike seats for comfort and tested the best massage gels for recovery. They looked for the best pillows and mattresses, so that riders would sleep well. They even changed the clothing for better airflow. Each change was almost too small to notice.

But small changes add up. Within a few years, British cyclists were winning Olympic gold medals by the handful, and later a British rider won the Tour de France, something that had never happened before.

The lesson is for us, too. Instead of one giant resolution, choose three small things in your personal and Jewish life, such as a few minutes of learning each day, a Shabbat candle, a kind call. A little each day, over a year, makes a very big gap between who we were and who we become.

And it is a good thought as we approach Rosh Hashanah: growth comes one small step at a time.

title: The Boy and the Fence
text:
There was once a little boy with a terrible temper. One day his father gave him a bag of nails. "Each time you lose your temper," he said, "hammer one nail into the back fence."

On the first day the boy hammered in fifty nails. But over the following weeks, the number fell. He found it was easier to hold his temper than to hammer all those nails. At last came a day when he did not lose his temper even once.

His father smiled. "Now," he said, "each day you keep your temper, pull one nail out."

The days passed, and finally the boy told his father that every nail was gone.

The father took his hand and led him to the fence. "You have done well, my son. But look at the holes. The fence will never be the same. When you speak in anger, your words leave marks like these. You can say sorry, and the wound may heal, but the scar remains."

Our Sages said much the same: words can hurt as deeply as a sword. Before we speak, we can take a breath. And when we have hurt someone, we can ask forgiveness, and mean it.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Fisherman Who Had Enough
text:
A fisherman docked his boat at eight in the morning with his hold half empty. A visitor asked why he had come in so early.

"I have caught enough for today," said the fisherman.

"But what will you do with the rest of the day?"

"Smoke my pipe, relax with my family, enjoy the quiet."

"Why not stay out longer and earn more?"

"What would I do with more money?"

"You could buy a second boat, then a whole fleet."

"And then what?"

"Then you could get really rich."

"And what would I do if I were rich?"

"Well, you could retire early."

"And what would I do then?"

The visitor hesitated. "Then you could do what you like. A little fishing, a pipe, time with your family, some quiet."

"That," said the fisherman, "is what I do already."

Our tradition does not tell us to stop working. But it does give us Shabbat, one day every week when we put down our tools and enjoy what we already have. As the Sages ask: who is rich? The one who is happy with his portion.
source: A well-known story, first written by Heinrich Böll in 1963

title: The Tablets That Carried Moses
text:
When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, he held two stone tablets engraved by G-d Himself. The Midrash tells us something wonderful about that descent.

The tablets were enormous and heavy, yet Moses did not struggle with them. The holy letters carved into the stone lifted them, and the tablets almost carried Moses down the mountain.

But as Moses came near the camp, he saw the Golden Calf, and the Sages say something astonishing happened. The letters could not remain beside an idol. They flew up out of the stone and returned to their Source.

Suddenly Moses held two blank slabs of stone, far too heavy for any man. He had to let them go, or be crushed beneath them. According to the Sages, he did not throw them down in rage. They slipped from his hands because the life had gone out of them.

The Rebbe added that, in truth, the letters themselves did not leave, only their living spirit.

There is a lesson in this for every Jew. When Torah is alive in our lives, it lifts us, and carrying it is a joy. When it becomes only a heavy tradition, a duty without meaning, it feels like a burden that is easy to drop. The way to keep the letters flying is to learn and to understand why we do what we do.
source: Chabad.org, "Why Did Moses Break the Tablets?"

title: The Garden That Was Left Free
text:
Two friends were talking about raising children. One said he did not believe in giving his children any religious education. "Their minds should be free," he explained. "When they grow up, they can choose for themselves."

His friend did not argue. He simply said, "Come, let me show you my garden."

The visitor followed him outside, expecting to see roses and fruit trees. Instead he found a tangle of weeds, thorns and tall grass.

"This is not a garden," he said in surprise. "It is nothing but weeds!"

"Well," said the host calmly, "I did not wish to interfere with my garden's freedom. I let it choose for itself what to grow."

The visitor understood. A garden does not become beautiful by being left alone. Someone has to plant and water it, and pull the weeds. The weeds, after all, need no help to grow.

The same is true for a child's heart. If we do not give our children Jewish values, stories, Shabbat and a sense of belonging, the world will happily fill the space with other things. Giving a child roots is not taking away freedom, but giving them something to choose from.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Deal of a Lifetime
text:
A businessman was offered the deal of a lifetime: forty million pounds, if he could be in Australia within two days to sign the contract in person.

He phoned his travel agent. Every flight was full for three days. He tried other agents, called the airline directly, even tried to charter a private plane. Nothing. In a panic he rushed to the airport, hoping for a standby seat, and still no luck.

Finally, he paid a member of the cabin crew twenty thousand pounds to let him hide in the airplane toilet for the twenty-five-hour flight.

So there he sat, in a tiny cramped space, while every few minutes someone knocked on the door.

Meanwhile, in first class, sat a millionaire so wealthy that he had nothing to do but fly around the world for the fun of it.

Now ask yourself: which of the two was happier?

The Torah's answer comes from the Sages: "Who is rich? One who is happy with his portion." Wealth is a blessing, and there is nothing wrong with earning it. But a person who is not content cannot be rich, and a person who cannot rest cannot enjoy what he has earned. That is part of the gift of Shabbat.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: "G-d Is Now Here"
text:
A father who wanted his young son to grow up without faith decided on a clever plan. One night, while the boy slept, he wrote three words on the headboard of his bed: "G-d is nowhere."

The next morning the little boy woke up and began to sound out the words, the way children do when they are just learning to read.

Then his face lit up. He jumped out of bed and ran to his father, shouting with excitement. "Daddy, Daddy! Look what's written on my bed! It says, 'G-d is now here!'"

What the father saw as an empty space, the child saw as a presence. Same letters, the same sentence, but a completely different message, depending on how we choose to look.

Jewish tradition says the same thing. The Baal Shem Tov taught that G-d is found everywhere, in every place and every moment. When we open our eyes the way a child does, we may find that the whole world is full of Him, and that He is now, and always, right here.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Archer Who Draws Afterward
text:
The Dubno Maggid, Rabbi Jacob Kranz, lived in Eastern Europe in the 1700s and was beloved for the parables he told to bring the Torah to life. People asked him how he always found the perfect story for every lesson.

He answered with a story of his own.

A man was walking through a forest when he noticed target circles painted on many trees. In the very center of every one stood an arrow. He was amazed. Who could be such a perfect archer?

Then he came upon a small boy playing, with a bow in his hand. "Do you know who shot these arrows?" he asked.

"I did," the boy replied.

The man could hardly believe it. "How?"

"It's simple," said the boy. "First I shoot the arrow. Then I draw the target around it."

"So it is with me," the Maggid said with a smile. "I first decide what lesson I want to teach, and then I build the story around it. And since every experience in life holds a lesson, I never run out of stories."

The story reminds us that if we look carefully, everything we meet in a day, a conversation, a small mishap, a moment of beauty, can teach us something, if we are ready to draw the target around it.
source: Wikipedia, "Jacob ben Wolf Kranz" (the Dubno Maggid)

title: Old Warwick and the Team
text:
A man was lost on a country road. Reaching for his map, he drifted off the road and landed in a muddy ditch. He was not hurt, but his car was stuck deep.

He walked to a nearby farm and asked for help. "Warwick can pull you out," said the farmer, pointing at a tired old mule in the field.

The man looked at the mule and doubted it. But he had no better idea.

The farmer hitched the mule to the car, snapped the reins and called out, "Pull, Fred! Pull, Jack! Pull, Ted! Pull, Warwick!" And the old mule pulled the car right out of the ditch.

The amazed driver thanked him, patted the mule, and asked, "Why did you call out all those names before Warwick's?"

The farmer smiled. "Old Warwick is almost blind. As long as he believes he is part of a team, he doesn't mind pulling."

Most of us pull a little harder when we feel we belong. That is what a community is for. At Chabad, as in any Jewish community, no one pulls alone, and every person is needed. The Sages said it simply: all of Israel are responsible for one another.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Oak and the Potato
text:
A prominent businessman was enrolling his son at a famous university. He looked through the long catalogue of courses and frowned.

"Does my son have to take all of these?" he asked the dean. "Can't you make it shorter? He wants to finish quickly."

"Certainly he can take a shorter course," said the dean. "It depends on what he wants to make of himself."

Then he added with a smile: "When G-d wants to make an oak tree, He takes twenty years. To make a potato, He needs only two months."

The things that matter most in life, character, wisdom, a strong Jewish soul, cannot be rushed. A child's education is not a sprint, and neither is our own growth. The Torah speaks of a person who is "like a tree planted by streams of water," growing slowly and steadily, bearing fruit in its time.

It is worth asking ourselves what we are growing: a quick potato, or an oak that will stand for generations.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: A Story on a Lap
text:
A successful businessman made it a rule to set aside time every evening to read his little daughter a bedtime story. It was the best part of her day, and of his.

One week he was especially busy, with meetings and late nights at the office. He did not want to disappoint her, so he came up with a solution. He recorded a series of stories on tape, so that she could listen to his voice at bedtime each night.

The next evening, the little girl came downstairs holding her pillow.

"Daddy," she said, "can you please read me a story?"

"But sweetheart, I recorded you a story. It's on the tape."

She looked at him with serious eyes. "Yes, Daddy. But the tape recorder can't take me on its lap and give me a hug."

He put down his work, picked her up, and read her a story.

Children do not measure love in minutes of content. They measure it in presence. Our Sages teach that giving someone your full attention is among the greatest kindnesses. Our Shabbat table is where many families rediscover this: phones away, and everyone together.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: Make Him Thirsty
text:
A young salesman was feeling discouraged. He had just lost an important sale, one he had worked on for weeks. He went to see his sales manager.

"I guess it just proves what they say," he sighed. "You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make it drink."

The manager shook his head kindly. "Son, let me give you some advice. Your job is not to make him drink. Your job is to make him thirsty."

The young man thought about it for a long time. It changed how he worked from then on. He stopped pushing, and started to ask what his customers really wanted.

The same applies to teaching our children, or sharing our heritage with a friend. We cannot force anyone to love Shabbat or the Torah. But we can show them how beautiful it is and let them taste a warm challah, hear a melody, see candles glowing. When people are thirsty, they find their way to the water on their own.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: When Brothers Act Like Brothers
text:
Two brothers had not spoken to each other for years. Something had come between them long ago, and neither would make the first move.

One day their elderly father came to visit. He stayed at the home of one brother. The other, hearing his father was in town, came over to see him. But when he walked in, he ignored his brother completely, as if he were not there.

He went up to his father and greeted him warmly. The old man looked back at him with a blank stare.

"Father, don't you recognize me?" the son asked, shocked. "I'm your son."

"Are you?" the father answered quietly. "Then you must be my son because I am staying with your brother, and yet you treat him like a stranger. When you act like brothers to each other, I will act like your father."

This is a story we hear around the High Holidays, when we call to G-d with the words "Avinu Malkeinu", "Our Father, our King." We ask Him to treat us as a loving father. But a father only feels like a father when his children are at peace with each other. Our relationship with G-d and our relationship with each other cannot be separated.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: David Hatuel Chose Life
text:
On May 2, 2004, Tali Hatuel was eight months pregnant, driving with her four young daughters near their home in Gush Katif, when terrorists attacked the car. Tali and all four girls were killed.

Her husband, David, was not in the car. He woke that morning as the father of a growing family, awaiting the birth of a baby boy. By the afternoon, his whole world had been taken from him.

It is hard even to imagine what that day was like. People who knew David said that he stood at a crossroads. He could let the grief swallow him, or he could stand up and keep living. He chose to live.

A year later he remarried, and he and his wife, Limor, began to build a new family. Their home filled with children again, and with it, with laughter.

David never said that the pain went away. But he showed what a person can do when life asks for the impossible: take the next step, and then the one after that.

Most of us will never face anything like this. So when we feel overwhelmed by our own troubles, David's story gives us a gentle thought. We are stronger than we believe, and there is always a way to go on.
source: Wikipedia, Murder of the Hatuel family

title: One Eye on the Road
text:
The story goes that Moshe Dayan, the famous Israeli general who wore a black patch over one eye, was once stopped for speeding.

The policeman recognized him at once. "General," he said, "someone like you should set an example for everyone else. I have to give you a ticket."

Dayan looked at him calmly. "Officer, you can see that I have only one eye. So tell me, which should I keep it on, the speedometer or the road?"

It is a funny answer, and it holds a real lesson. Many of us keep our eyes so tightly on the speedometer, on how fast we are going and how we measure up, that we forget to look at the road ahead.

How we are getting there matters. But where we are going matters even more. Once in a while, it is worth lifting our eyes and asking whether we are heading somewhere that we truly want to reach. A little time spent on that question can save a lot of wandering.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Elephant and the Small Chain
text:
Have you ever watched a circus elephant? It weighs several tons, yet it stands patiently, held by a thin chain tied to a small wooden stake. With one step, it could snap the chain and walk away. Why doesn't it?

The tale explains it this way. When the elephant was a baby, it was tied with the very same chain. It pulled and pulled, with all its little might, but the stake did not budge. After many days of trying, it gave up.

And then something quiet happened. The elephant came to believe that the chain could not be broken. It grew into a giant, but the memory of those early failures stayed with it. It no longer tests the chain, because it is certain the answer is no.

How many of us are tied to a small stake like that? Something we tried when we were young, or when we were less ready, did not work out, and we decided we could never do it. Perhaps it was learning to pray, to keep Shabbat, to forgive, or to change.

Our Sages teach that a person is never too old to begin, and never too weak to try again. Give the chain one more pull. You may be stronger than you think.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The City Without Water
text:
About five hundred years ago, the Mughal emperor Akbar the Great decided to build a new capital in northern India. He chose a site called Fatehpur Sikri and spent a fortune on it.

The city was breathtaking. It had palaces, courtyards, gardens and great halls, built of red sandstone and marble, blending the best of Persian and Hindu design.

But the court lived there for only about fourteen years. According to many historians, the city simply did not have enough water. Whatever the exact reasons, the emperor and his court left, and the magnificent capital was abandoned.

Today Fatehpur Sikri is one of the most visited sites in India. It stands there, beautiful and silent, a city with everything except what it needed most.

Our Sages compare Torah to water. Without water, nothing can live, no matter how impressive it looks. A Jewish life, a family or a community can have wonderful buildings, successes and plans. But without the quiet, steady flow of Torah to nourish it, it cannot last.

The good news is that this water is free and always near. A few minutes of learning each day, a Shabbat meal, a blessing said with a smile: these are how we keep our own city alive.

title: The Woman Who Searched for Herself
text:
In August 2012, a bus full of tourists stopped near a volcanic canyon in Iceland called Eldgja. When they got back on board, the guide counted heads and found one passenger missing.

The police were alerted, and about fifty people set out in the dark to look for her. A rescue helicopter was grounded by fog, so the tourists searched on foot. The description they were given was of a woman in dark clothes.

One of the searchers was a tourist who had changed her clothes since the stop. She did not recognize herself in the description, so she joined the search with everyone else.

Hours passed, until around three in the morning it finally became clear that the missing woman was not missing at all. She had been looking for herself the whole night.

It is a funny story, but it has a serious side. Many of us spend years searching for something, meaning, belonging, our place, without realizing that we are the one we have been looking for.

Our teachers say that every Jew carries a deep, holy soul that never goes missing. It may be dressed in different clothes, so that we hardly recognize it. But it is always there, and we can find it at any moment, especially in the days of return before Yom Kippur.

title: You Know the Psalm, I Know the Shepherd
text:
At a concert, a world-famous singer was asked to perform Psalm 23, "The Lord is my shepherd." He sang it magnificently. His voice soared, every note was perfect, and the audience rose to its feet with thunderous applause.

Then an old Jewish man in the back stood up. He did not have a polished voice. It was rough and cracked, and he stumbled over a few words. But as he recited the psalm, people began to cry. By the end, the whole room was in tears.

Afterward, the singer came over to him, puzzled. "I don't understand," he said. "I sang it beautifully, and they applauded. You sang it, and they wept. What is the difference?"

The old man smiled gently. "It is simple," he said. "You know the psalm. I know the Shepherd."

Our prayers do not need a beautiful voice or perfect pronunciation. What opens hearts, our own and others', is how close we feel to the One we are talking to. When we pray like a child speaking to a loving parent, even a few simple words can reach all the way to heaven.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Deaf Husband and the Blind Wife
text:
The story is told of a couple who had been happily married for many years, though on the surface they seemed a poor match.

The husband was far from handsome, and his wife was a sharp-tongued woman who complained from morning to night. But the wife was blind, and the husband was deaf. She pictured a tall, handsome man at her side. And whenever she grumbled, he imagined she was saying something sweet.

One day the husband read about a doctor who could cure even the most serious impairments. "Let's go," they agreed. "Why live with less than we could have?"

The operations were a complete success. The husband could hear, and the wife could see.

And their marriage fell apart within weeks. She saw the husband she had actually married, and he finally heard what she had actually been saying.

The tale is a smile with a serious point. We often think, "If only my situation were different, everything would be better." But life is not always improved by changing our circumstances. G-d gave each of us particular strengths and weaknesses. Our work is to make the best of what we have, and to look kindly at the people around us, flaws and all.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: I Am Jealous of You
text:
Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev was known as the great defender of the Jewish people. He always looked for the good in everyone.

One day he met a man in town who was known for living far from Torah and mitzvot, and who seemed to take pride in it. The Rebbe looked at him warmly and said, "I am jealous of you."

The man was shocked. "Jealous of me? Why?"

"Because of what you will have when you do teshuvah, when you return," said the Rebbe. "When someone comes back to G-d out of love, our Sages teach that even the wrong things he did can be turned into merits. Think of how much good you will have to your name. I have never had the chance to turn so much around."

The man had expected a lecture. Instead he had been told that nothing in his past could shut the door. That the whole of his life, even the broken parts, could become light.

That is the Chassidic view of every Jew. Nobody is beyond reach, nobody is a lost cause, and a past full of mistakes is not a wall but raw material. When we return with love, G-d does not only forgive. He helps us transform.

It is a message especially for the days before Yom Kippur, but it is true all year round.

title: The Last House He Built
text:
Moshe was a master builder. Everything he built stood tall and strong, and people came from far away to praise his work.

When he was ready to retire, he told his boss, the contractor, that he was looking forward to a long, well-earned vacation with his wife. But on his very last week, the contractor came to him with one more request. “Just one more house, Moshe. There is no one I trust like you.”

Moshe agreed, but his heart was already on the vacation. For the first time in his life he cut corners. He measured carelessly, used poor materials and rushed to finish. The house he put up was full of cracks and creaks, the kind that would not last through a storm.

When it was done, the contractor shook his hand. “Moshe, you have given me many years of wonderful work. This house is my gift to you.” And he handed him the key.

Moshe had built his own home.

Our Sages teach that the way we treat others comes back to us. The care we give to our parents, our family and our community is the house we will one day live in.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: Good Morning, Herr Mueller
text:
Before the war, a Chassidic rabbi in Poland loved to greet everyone he met. On his daily walk he would pass a neighbor named Herr Mueller, tip his hat and say warmly, “Good morning, Herr Mueller!” Mueller, who was proud to be greeted so respectfully by the rabbi, would answer, “Good morning, Herr Rabbiner!”

Then the war came. The walks stopped. Friends turned away, neighbors disappeared, and Mueller put on the uniform of the Nazis.

Years later, in Auschwitz, the rabbi stood in a line of prisoners waiting to be sorted. One gesture of an officer’s hand sent a person to the left, to death, and another to the right, to life. The rabbi was old and weak, and he knew very well which way his hand would point.

When he reached the front, he looked up and saw the officer’s face. It was Herr Mueller.

The rabbi stood straight, as he always had, and softly said, “Good morning, Herr Mueller.”

The officer froze. Then, very quietly, he answered, “Good morning, Herr Rabbiner.” And his hand pointed to the right.

The story comes from Yaffa Eliach’s collection of Chassidic tales of the Holocaust, who wrote it down from an elderly Chassidic man. It reminds us that a simple greeting, given every day, never goes to waste.
source: Hasidic Tales of the Holocaust by Yaffa Eliach (also retold on Breslev.co.il)

title: The Cat Is on the Roof
text:
Phil had never taken a day off in his life. He cared for his elderly mother and his beloved cat, and finally his family convinced him to take a long vacation. His brother promised to look after both.

On the first day, Phil called to ask about the cat. “I’m so sorry,” said his brother. “The cat died. It ran into the street.”
