Phil was heartbroken. “You have to learn how to tell people bad news,” he said. “You could have prepared me. First you say, ‘The cat is on the roof.’ The next day, ‘We’re having trouble getting the cat down.’ The day after, ‘I’m sorry, the cat fell.’ That way I would have known something was coming.”

His brother apologized and promised to do better.

“Now,” said Phil, “how is Mom?”

There was a long pause. “Well,” said his brother, “Mom is on the roof.”

The lesson: kindness matters, but so does clarity. If we are so careful not to speak directly that no one understands us, we do not help anyone. Speak gently, but speak honestly.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Two Yuds
text:
A little boy had just started learning Chumash, the Five Books of Moses, in cheder, the traditional Jewish school. He had been taught that two letters yud written together stand for Hashem’s holy name, and so whenever he saw them, he would say “Hashem.”

One day, reading aloud, he ended every verse with “Hashem.” The teacher stopped him. “Why do you say that?”

The boy pointed. “Look, Rebbe. At the end of every verse there are two yuds!” He was seeing the two dots, like a colon, that mark the end of a verse.

The teacher smiled. Those dots are not G-d’s name, he explained, but the boy had noticed something wonderful. A yud can also stand for a Yid, a Jew. When two Jews stand side by side, as friends and equals, G-d’s presence rests between them. But when one stands above the other, looking down on his friend, the two yuds are just the end of the verse. The shining stops.

The story is told in Chassidic tradition, often in the name of Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz, who taught that where there is true unity, there is G-d.
source: Chabad.org (“Harmony”), a story told in Chassidic tradition

title: Write It in Sand, Carve It in Stone
text:
Two friends were walking through the desert. Somewhere along the way they began to argue, and one of them struck the other across the face.

The one who was hit said nothing. He knelt and wrote in the sand: “Today my best friend hit me.”

They walked on until they reached an oasis and went in to bathe. The friend who had been hit got stuck in the mud and began to sink. The other friend pulled him out and saved his life.

When he had recovered, he took a stone and carved: “Today my best friend saved my life.”

The friend who had struck him asked, “Why did you write the first in sand and the second in stone?”

He answered, “When someone hurts us, we should write it in sand, where the winds of forgiveness can blow it away. But when someone does us good, we should carve it in stone, where no wind can erase it.”

The Torah asks us to love our neighbor and not to hold a grudge. This story shows how: let the hurts fade, and remember the kindness.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Boy With the Books
text:
One Friday, a high school freshman noticed a classmate named Kyle walking home carrying every book he owned. “What a nerd,” he thought, and kept walking.

Then he saw a group of boys knock the books out of Kyle’s arms and send him sprawling in the dirt. His glasses flew into the grass. The freshman saw the sadness in Kyle’s eyes, ran over, helped him find his glasses and picked up the books. They talked all the way home. Kyle turned out to be funny and kind, and the two became best friends.

Years later, at graduation, Kyle stood up as the top student of the class to give his speech. He thanked his parents and teachers, and then said that the best gift is to be a friend. He told the story of the day they met. He had planned to take his own life that weekend, which is why he was taking his things home. One kind boy, who just stopped to help, had changed his mind.

The friend stared. He had never known.

The story reminds us that a small act of kindness can change a life, and that we rarely know how much it matters. Our Sages say that saving one life is like saving an entire world. Often it begins by simply stopping to help.

If you or someone you love is struggling, please reach out to someone you trust. The Rabbi is always here to listen.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: Be a Player, Not a Fan
text:
In 1955, a boy about to become Bar Mitzvah came with his father to see the Lubavitcher Rebbe at 770 Eastern Parkway in Brooklyn. In those years, boys often met the Rebbe privately before their Bar Mitzvah to receive a blessing.

The Rebbe asked about his birthday, tested him on what he was studying, and gave him a blessing. Then he surprised everyone. “Are you a baseball fan?”

The boy said he was, and that he rooted for the Dodgers. The Rebbe asked whether he went to games. Yes, the boy said, a month ago. “How was it?” Disappointing, he admitted. By the sixth inning the Dodgers were losing nine to two, so they left.

“Did the players leave also?” asked the Rebbe.

The boy was startled. “Of course not. The players can’t leave in the middle of the game!”

“Why not?”

“Because they are in the game. Fans can leave whenever they like. The players have to stay until the end and keep trying to win.”

The Rebbe smiled. “In the game of life, there are two kinds of people. Some watch from the stands, and some play. Take this lesson with you: be a player.”

The story is told on Chabad.org.

title: The Brick and the Jaguar
text:
A successful young executive was driving through a quiet neighborhood in his brand-new Jaguar, a little too fast. He watched for children darting out between parked cars. None appeared. But suddenly a brick slammed into the side door.

He slammed on the brakes, backed up and jumped out. He grabbed the first boy he saw and pushed him against a car. “What are you doing? That’s a new car, and that brick will cost a fortune!”

“Please, mister, I’m sorry,” the boy said, with tears running down his face. “I didn’t know what else to do. No one would stop.” He pointed. “It’s my brother. He rolled off the curb and fell out of his wheelchair, and I can’t lift him. Please, can you help?”

The man swallowed hard. He lifted the boy’s brother back into the chair, wiped his scrapes with a handkerchief and made sure he was all right. “Thank you, and G-d bless you,” the boy said.

The man watched them walk home. It was a long, slow walk back to his car. He never fixed the dent. It reminded him not to go through life so fast that someone has to throw a brick to get his attention.

Sometimes G-d whispers to us. When we don’t listen, we may hear Him in a louder way.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: A Shofar for the Children
text:
This story is told every year before Rosh Hashanah. It is a hard story, and it is told with great respect.

It is said that on the eve of Rosh Hashanah in Auschwitz, a group of Jewish children sat huddled in their barracks, whispering. They knew what lay ahead. One of them, perhaps only eight years old, said, “Tomorrow is Rosh Hashanah. We must hear the shofar before it is too late.”

A message was passed in secret to the men’s barracks, where a rabbi had managed to hide a shofar. The next morning, at great risk, the rabbi came and blew it for the children.

When the last note faded, one of the children said, “Rabbi, we want you to know that we will die believing in G-d.”

The story is told on Chabad.org and elsewhere, but without names or dates, and we cannot confirm it. It is told to remind us of the pure faith of Jewish children, and of the parents and teachers who gave it to them. Whatever each of us believes, we are asked to listen to the shofar, and to remember.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed

title: The Minister of Defence
text:
When Margaret Thatcher was Britain’s Secretary of State for Education, she met the Chief Rabbi of the United Kingdom, Rabbi Immanuel Jakobovits. In the conversation, he told her something she never forgot: “You are really the Minister of Defence.”

He explained what he meant. After what children learn at home, it is what they learn in school that keeps a nation whole and strong.

Years later, in 1991, she recalled the remark in a speech at a dinner honoring Rabbi Jakobovits on his retirement as Chief Rabbi. She said it carried special meaning for the Jewish people. The Jews are a small people, scattered across the world. Where other nations relied on armies and statecraft to survive, the Jewish people relied mainly on learning. Education has been our greatest defense.

That is why a Jewish child learning the alef-bet, a family around the Shabbat table, and a Hebrew school class in Lafayette, Moraga or Orinda are not small things. They are how the Jewish people has always protected its future.
source: Margaret Thatcher’s speech at Rabbi Jakobovits’ retirement dinner (margaretthatcher.org), also reported by JTA

title: The Parrot in the Window
text:
A soccer fan kept walking past a pet shop where a parrot in the window squawked insults about his favorite team. After the third time, he stormed in and told the owner, “One more word out of that bird and I’ll finish him!”

The worried owner went to his rabbi, who happened to have an identical parrot, and asked to swap birds for a couple of weeks. The rabbi agreed.

The next afternoon the fan marched past the window and again growled the insult at the parrot. The bird looked at him calmly and answered, “May G-d answer your prayers. May G-d answer your prayers.”

title: A Quick Bite at Oleinu
text:
A man from a tiny village found himself in a big-city shul for Yom Kippur. During the Aleinu prayer he was amazed to see everyone cover their heads with their tallit and bow to the floor. “What’s going on?” he whispered. His neighbor said, “Oh, we all grab a quick bite under there.”

The next year the visitor came prepared, with a chicken drumstick in his pocket. When everyone bowed, he covered himself and dug in. Long after the congregation stood up, he was still on the floor, munching away.

When he finally came up, someone asked what he’d been doing down there. He looked surprised. “Some people are quick eaters,” he said, “and some take longer!”

title: Paid Up and Sleeping
text:
A man dozed off in shul and began to snore. The shammas, the synagogue caretaker, tapped his shoulder. “Please, sir, you’re disturbing the others.”

“Listen,” the man said crossly, “I paid my dues for the whole year, and I’ll do what I like!”

“Of course, sir,” said the shammas gently. “But you’re keeping everyone else awake.”

title: The Fisherman Comes to Shul
text:
A man who used to spend every Shabbat morning fishing suddenly started coming faithfully to shul. The rabbi was delighted, and after services he said, “How wonderful to see you here with your good wife each week!”

The man shrugged. “Well, Rabbi, to be honest, it’s a matter of choice. I’d rather hear your sermon than hers.”

title: The Boy Who Wanted to Be a Rabbi
text:
A young boy decided he wanted to be a rabbi when he grew up, so his parents sent him to interview their own rabbi. “Ask me anything about the rabbinate,” the rabbi said grandly.

“Well,” said the boy, “besides giving a fifteen-minute sermon on Shabbat morning, what do you do all week?”

The rabbi nearly shouted. “You don’t want to be a rabbi! With questions like that, you should be the shul president!”

title: The Blessing on the Watermelon
text:
At a Shabbaton in Israel, a rabbi heard a guest make the blessing Shehakol over a slice of watermelon. He gently noted that for fruit of the ground the right one is Ha’adamah.

“I know,” said the man, “but I say Shehakol.” They went back and forth until the rabbi asked why.

“I served in a tank unit in the Yom Kippur War,” the man said. “We were surrounded. The commander asked if anyone knew how to pray, and one fellow knew just one thing: Shehakol. He shouted it, and we knocked out an enemy tank. We kept it up and all of us came home alive. If Shehakol was good enough for tanks, it’s good enough for watermelon!”

title: A Very Resourceful Visitor
text:
Becky belonged to a shul group that visits and helps sick members, and one day, on her rounds, she ran out of gas. The nearby station’s only gas can was out on loan, and she was already late for her next patient.

Then she spotted the bedpan she always kept in the car for patients. Resourceful as ever, she carried it to the station, filled it with gas, and walked back to her car, which was covered in Hebrew decals and bumper stickers.

As she poured the gas into her tank, two men across the street watched in amazement. One turned to the other and said, “If that car starts, I’m becoming Jewish tomorrow!”

title: Moishe Parks His Car
text:
Chana was the self-appointed guardian of the shul’s morals, forever poking her nose into other people’s business. Everyone put up with her. Then she made a mistake: she saw new member Moishe’s car parked outside the town’s only bar one afternoon, and loudly announced that everyone driving by would know what he was up to.

Moishe, a man of few words, looked at her for a moment and walked away. He didn’t explain or defend himself.

That evening he quietly parked his car in front of Chana’s house, walked home, and left it there all night.

title: A Question for Mount Sinai
text:
Did you know Moshe made a third trip up Mount Sinai? After a long climb, he took off his shoes, knelt, and said, “Master of the Universe, Your people sent me back with a question about the Ten Commandments.”

“What is it?” boomed the voice of G-d.

“They want to know,” said Moshe, “whether the commandments are listed in order of priority.”

title: A Eulogy with a Catch
text:
Issy and Howard were wealthy brothers whom no one in town liked. When Issy died, Howard went to Rabbi Bloom. “I’ll donate a million dollars to the shul,” he said, “if at the funeral you say my brother was a mensch.”

The rabbi thought long and hard, and agreed.

At the funeral, he spoke at length about everything Issy had done wrong. Then he finished: “But compared to his brother, he was a mensch!”

title: Sunday Brunch and a Storm
text:
Yankel and Sheina were on their shul’s welcoming committee, so they invited new neighbors Abe and Sarah for Sunday brunch. Afterward the women went shopping, and Yankel took Abe out on his sailboat.

A storm blew up. The tide went out, the boat ran aground in a narrow channel, and the two men had to climb overboard and shove with all their strength.

Abe stood ankle-deep in mud, wind whipping his hair, rain streaming down his face. He grinned at Yankel and said, “Sure beats shopping.”

title: Fluent in Japanese in Ten Days
text:
Two Jewish soldiers were stationed in Japan after the war. One morning one of them woke up and said in Yiddish, “Abe, shtay oif, der zun shaynt!” That means, “Abe, get up, the sun is shining!”

A soldier from another unit overheard and shook his head in admiration. “Those two are amazing,” he said. “Ten days in this country, and they’re already speaking Japanese!”

title: A Foolproof Business Plan
text:
A poor man talked his way into an appointment with a wealthy philanthropist by promising a sure way to make five million dollars.

“Nu, let’s hear it,” said the philanthropist.

“It’s simple,” said the visitor. “I hear that when your daughter marries, you’re giving her a ten-million-dollar dowry. So I’ve come to tell you that I’m willing to marry her for half!”

title: Rescue at the Duck Pond
text:
A man was feeding the ducks at a park pond when he saw a dog struggling in the water. Before he could move, a Jewish gentleman sitting nearby had handed his coat to his wife, his hat to his son, and his shoes to his daughter, and leaped in. He hauled the dog to shore and even gave it mouth-to-mouth. The dog shook itself, licked its rescuer’s face, and ran off wagging its tail.

Amazed, the onlooker walked over. “That was wonderful. Are you a vet?”

“A vet?” the man answered. “Can’t you see? I’m wet!”

title: A Generous Donation
text:
A traffic safety consultant gave a talk to a parents’ group. Afterward the program chairwoman thanked him warmly and handed him a check for fifty dollars.

“Speaking is part of my job,” he said. “May I donate this to one of your causes?”

“How wonderful!” she said. “We have the perfect project. We’re trying to raise money so we can afford better speakers.”

title: The Matchmaker Has an Answer
text:
Blanche Gurfein, a pillar of her community, took pride in her matchmaking. One day Mr. Greenthal, a divorced man, called her up.

“Blanche! That widow you talked me into dating?”

“A wonderful woman,” said Blanche.

“Wonderful? She has a terrible limp!”

“Only when she walks!” snapped the shadchente.

title: The Price of a Specialist
text:
Dr. Levine, a famous specialist, finished examining Nathan. “What do I owe you?” asked Nathan.

“Twenty-five dollars.”

“Twenty-five! Too much. I don’t have it.”

“Fifteen, then.”

“Fifteen? Out of the question!”

“Five?”

“Who has five dollars? I’m a poor man!”

The doctor lost patience. “If you have nothing, how dare you come to an expensive specialist?”

“For my health,” cried Nathan, thumping his chest, “nothing is too expensive!”

title: Who Asked Whom?
text:
A widower and a widow, high school classmates, met again at their sixtieth reunion. They had a lovely evening, and finally he gathered his courage and asked, “Will you marry me?”

After about six seconds she said, “Yes. Yes, I will!”

The next morning he was troubled. Had she said yes or no? He couldn’t remember. Nervously, he phoned her, explained that his memory wasn’t what it used to be, and asked.

“You silly man,” she said, “I said yes, and I meant it with all my heart! And I’m so glad you called, because I couldn’t remember who asked me!”

title: Sadie’s Headache
text:
Sadie went to see her rabbi and spent hours complaining about her terrible headaches and her difficult life. Suddenly she cried out happily, “Rabbi, your holy presence has cured me! My headache is gone!”

“No, Sadie,” said the rabbi. “It’s not gone. I have it now.”

title: Sammy and the Stock Market
text:
Young Sammy asked his father, “Papa, what is the stock market?”

“You’re too young to understand,” said Papa. But Sammy insisted. “I don’t want to start poor like you, selling secondhand clothes. I want to know now!”

So Papa explained. “You buy two chickens. They lay eggs, the eggs hatch, and soon you have thousands of chickens. That’s the stock market. Understand? Then one day the sky opens, it rains like in Noah’s time, and the flood washes the chickens away. You’re left with two or three. That is also the stock market.”

He sighed. “You should have bought ducks.”

title: The Exchange Policy
text:
The judge frowned at the weary burglar. “You admit breaking into the same store three nights in a row?”

“Yes, Your Honor.”

“Why?”

“My wife wanted a dress.”

The judge checked his papers. “But it says here three nights in a row!”

“Yes, sir,” sighed the man. “She made me exchange it twice.”

title: Count Your Blessings
text:
A group of seniors sat around comparing ailments. “My arms are so weak I can barely lift my coffee,” said one. “My cataracts are so bad I can’t even see my coffee,” said another. “My hands are so stiff I couldn’t sign my name,” said a third. “I can’t turn my head,” said a fourth. “My pills make me dizzy,” said a fifth. “I forget where I’m going,” said a sixth.

“Well, that’s the price of getting older,” sighed an old man, and they all nodded.

“Count your blessings,” said one woman cheerfully. “Thank G-d we can all still drive!”

title: Two Words a Year
text:
A Jewish man joined a retreat for deeply spiritual people. The head guru told him he must take a vow of silence, with one exception: once a year he could speak two words to the guru.

After a year of backbreaking work in the vineyards, he stood before the guru and said, “Bed hard.” “Thank you for your input,” said the guru. “Back to work.”

Another year passed, and he had grown thin. “Food bad,” he said. “Thank you again,” said the guru. “Back to work.”

A third year passed. “I quit,” said the man.

“I’m not surprised,” said the guru. “You’ve done nothing but complain since you got here.”

title: Who Delivered the Tablets?
text:
G-d stood at the foot of Mount Sinai, and Moshe had just come down. The two tablets lay shattered in a thousand pieces.

“What have you done?” G-d demanded. “Didn’t I tell you to deliver the Ten Commandments to the children of Israel?”

“Yes, Lord,” said Moshe. “But a man in a brown uniform, in a flying brown chariot with gold letters on the side, appeared on the mountain and said he would deliver them. I thought You sent him.”

“I certainly did not,” said G-d. “What were the letters on the chariot?”

Moshe bent down and wrote three letters in the sand: U-P-S. Then he pronounced them: “Oops.”

title: Anyone Here Know How to Pray?
text:
The storm raged, and the captain realized his ship was sinking fast. “Does anyone here know how to pray?” he shouted.

One man stepped forward. “Aye, Captain, I do.”

“Good,” said the captain. “You pray, and the rest of us will put on life jackets. We’re one short.”

title: The Patient Waiter
text:
Estelle Rosenstein, a regular at a Miami restaurant popular with seniors, was bothering the waiter again. First she asked him to turn up the air conditioning because she was too hot, then to turn it down because she was too cold, and so on for half an hour.

The waiter stayed calm and kept smiling. Finally another customer asked why he didn’t simply tell her off.

“Oh, I don’t mind,” said the waiter with a smile. “We don’t even have an air conditioner.”

title: Anything to Declare?
text:
Flying home from France, I noticed a worn-out mother heading into customs with eight children, all under ten, and a mountain of suitcases. A young customs officer watched in disbelief. “Ma’am, do all these children and this luggage belong to you?”

“Yes, sir,” she sighed.

“Do you have any weapons, contraband or drugs?”

“Sir,” she answered calmly, “if I’d had any of those, I would have used them by now.”

title: Which Tire Was It?
text:
Four yeshiva students were top of their Talmud class and confident about Monday’s final. So they spent Sunday partying with friends in another city, planning to be back in time. But they overslept, and only got home Monday afternoon.

They went to the rabbi with a story: a flat tire on the way back, no spare, and they had to wait for the garage to open. The rabbi kindly let them take the exam the next morning.

They studied hard all night. Next day he put each in a separate room. The first question, worth five percent, was easy. Relieved, each turned the page to the second question, worth ninety-five percent:

“Which tire was it?”

title: Why the House Stayed Warm
text:
John and Mary Smith bought an old house in upstate New York from Sadie and Alfred Horowitz. Winter was coming, and the house had no insulation. But John was confident. “If they lived here all those years, so can we!”

One November night the temperature dropped below zero, and the Smiths woke up to frost on the inside walls. John phoned the Horowitzes and asked how they had kept the house warm. After a short conversation he hung up and muttered to Mary, “Turns out for the last thirty years they went to Florida every winter.”

title: The Name Sarah
text:
A father and his little girl joined us for services at our Chabad House. During the kiddush, I bent down and asked her, “What’s your name?”

“Sarah,” she said.

“What a special name! Do you know a very special woman in Jewish history was named Sarah?” I got a blank look, so I went on: “She was the wife of a famous man, the very first Jew, named Abraham.”

Her face lit up. “I didn’t know Abraham Lincoln was Jewish!”

Her blushing father, an attorney, looked at me and said, “Great sense of humor!”

title: Dad’s Advice for a First Date
text:
A young man got advice from his father before his first date. “If you run out of things to say, remember the three Fs: family, food, and philosophy.”

He met the girl, and within a minute they had nothing to say. So he tried the three Fs. “Do you have brothers or sisters?”

“No.”

On to the second F. “Do you like gefilte fish?”

“No.”

Getting desperate, he asked, “Well, if you had a brother or sister, do you think they would have liked gefilte fish?”

title: Seven Weeks
text:
A couple having marriage trouble went to see the rabbi, hoping to save their very young marriage.

“What brought you to this point?” the rabbi asked the husband.

“In the six weeks we’ve been together,” the husband said, “we haven’t agreed on a single thing.”

“Seven weeks,” said the wife.

title: Moishele Plays Football
text:
A Jewish quarterback at the University of Michigan invited his immigrant parents to watch him play. They had no idea what their son did at college, but they were bursting with pride.

From the fifty-yard line, they watched in horror as huge, hulking players kept piling onto their boy. At halftime he came over. “So, Ma and Pa, what do you think?”

His father said, “Moishele, just give them the ball already, and I’ll buy you a new one!”

title: Two Principles for Business
text:
A man retiring from the garment business handed it over to his son. “It’s all yours,” he said. “I made a good living because of two principles: honesty and wisdom. Honesty means that if you promise the goods by the first of April, then no matter what happens in the shop, you deliver by the first of April.”

“Sure, Dad,” said the son. “And wisdom?”

“The wisest thing you can do,” said his father, “is never make any promises.”

title: The Flowers and the Check
text:
A man ordered flowers for his anniversary, but they arrived as closed buds. He phoned the florist to complain. “Give it a few days,” he was told. “They’ll open by themselves.”

“And if they don’t?”

“Then feel free to open them yourself.”

Three days later the florist called back, furious. “There’s no money in the bank account behind your check!”

“Ah,” said the man, “it’s a special kind of check. Give it a few days, and the account will open by itself.”

“And if it doesn’t?”

“Nu, then feel free to open one yourself.”

title: I Know What the Bible Means
text:
A rabbi’s little son ran up to him proudly. “Tatte, I know what the Bible means!”

The rabbi smiled. “What do you mean, you know what the Bible means?”

“I do!”

“All right. What does it mean?”

“That’s easy, Tatte,” said the boy excitedly. “B-I-B-L-E: Basic Information Before Leaving Earth!”

title: The Matchmaker’s Fine Print
text:
A shadchan, a matchmaker, assured a prospective groom that the girl came from a fine family, though sadly her father, alav hashalom, was no longer alive.

During the engagement the young man discovered that the father was very much alive, but serving a prison sentence. He ran to the shadchan. “How could you lie? Why did you tell me her father was dead?”

“Nu,” said the shadchan, “do you call that living?”

title: Baruch Hashem!
text:
After school, first-grader Moishie Rothman was eating his snack at the kitchen table when he announced, “Mom, my teacher asked if I have any brothers or sisters who will be coming to school.”

“That’s nice of her to take an interest,” said his mother. “What did she say when you told her you don’t have any yet?”

“She just said, ‘Baruch Hashem!’”

title: Until a Hundred and Twenty
text:
At a dinner for seniors, old Mr. Cohen went around the room asking people their age. The first said he was ninety. “Wonderful!” said Mr. Cohen. “Bis hundert un tzvantzig!” That is the Yiddish blessing, “Until a hundred and twenty!”

The next said he was nearly a hundred. “Bis hundert un tzvantzig!” said Mr. Cohen again.

The third said, “I’m a hundred and twenty today.”

“Well,” said Mr. Cohen, “have a good day.”

title: Schmerel Visits the Big City
text:
Before the war, many Jews lived their whole lives in a village that was ninety percent Jewish. For some, the only contact with non-Jews was the “Shabbos goy,” a neighbor who came on Shabbat mornings in winter to light the stove, which Jews may not do on Shabbat.

Schmerel, a villager, once had to visit the big city. He marveled at the tall buildings, the factories and the roads. But what astonished him most was how few Jews there were compared to everyone else.

He turned to a fellow Jew and exclaimed, “Why on earth do you need so many Shabbos goys?”

title: The Family Condition
text:
Chaim Epstein was at the doctor for his annual checkup. “I know what you’re going to say,” said Chaim. “High blood pressure.”

“You got it,” said Dr. Rosenberg. “Do you get it from your mother’s side or your father’s side?”

“Neither,” said Chaim. “My wife’s side.”

“How can you get this from your wife’s family?”

“Oy,” said Chaim, “you should meet them sometime!”

title: Daddy Daycare
text:
Chaim worked long hours, and his wife Rochel complained that he wasn’t spending enough time with their three-year-old, Rivka. So Chaim took little Rivka to the mall and even gave her a ride on his shoulders.

After a few minutes, Rivka started tugging at his hair. “Stop that, honey,” said Chaim. “It hurts.”

“But Daddy,” she said, “I’m only trying to get my gum back.”

title: The Kippah That Never Fails
text:
David was driving down the highway when he saw a man in a kippah standing beside a broken-down car. He pulled over to help. While working on the car, he noticed a cross hanging around the man’s neck.

Unable to hold back his curiosity, David asked, “Are you Jewish, by any chance?”

“No, not at all.”

“Then what’s with the skullcap?”

“Oh, that. My mother gave it to me years ago. She said if I ever got stuck on the highway, I should put this on and I’d get help in no time. It hasn’t failed me yet.”

title: The Man Who Cried at Hava Nagila
text:
The Hebrew school held a talent show for the community. A girl played Hava Nagila on the piano, and a grandmother noticed the man next to her wiping his eyes.

“Isn’t it beautiful,” she whispered, “that our young people are carrying on our tradition?”

“I’m not Jewish,” said the man.

“Then why are you crying?”

“I’m a musician.”

title: Chanukah Shopping Before the Crowds
text:
It was Chanukah, and the judge was in a merry mood. “What are you charged with?” he asked the defendant.

“Doing my Chanukah shopping early, Your Honor.”

“That’s no offense,” said the judge. “How early were you shopping?”

“Before the store opened.”

title: A Career Change
text:
Joshua was a successful salesman at Levine’s Tailors, always so polite that nearly everyone who walked in left with a suit. So it was a surprise when, after ten years, he quit to join the police force.

His father couldn’t understand it. At the end of Joshua’s first week, he called to ask how it was going.

“Thanks for asking, Dad,” said Joshua. “The pay is okay, the hours are better than I expected, and my colleagues are great. But what I like best is that here, the customer is always wrong.”

title: Punished for Something I Didn’t Do
text:
Little Rivkah came home from school and told her mother, “Mommy, today I was punished for something I didn’t do.”

“That’s terrible!” said her mother. “I’m going to speak to your teacher! By the way, what was it that you didn’t do?”

“My homework,” said Rivkah.

title: Letters from College
text:
Miriam was bragging to her neighbor Esther about her son at college. “He’s so brilliant,” she said, “that every time we get a letter from him, we have to look in the dictionary.”

“You’re lucky,” said Esther. “Every time we get a letter from ours, we have to go to the bank!”

title: The College Graduate and the Broom
text:
Moishe Goldberg, owner of Moishe’s Kosher Grocer, did his friend Herb a favor and hired Herb’s grandson David, fresh out of college. On David’s first day, Moishe greeted him with a warm handshake, handed him a broom, and said, “Your first job is to sweep the store.”

“But I’m a college graduate,” David protested.

“Oh, I’m sorry, I didn’t know,” said Moishe. “Here, give me the broom. I’ll show you how.”

title: Never Lend to Your Children
text:
Moshe asked his friend Chaim to borrow his lawn mower.

“I’d love to,” said Chaim, “but I just lent it to my son.”

“Never lend anything to your children,” said Moshe. “They never return it.”

“Oh, it’s fine,” said Chaim. “The ladder I lent him isn’t mine. It’s my father’s!”

title: Science Class with Mrs. Cohen
text:
Mrs. Cohen was teaching her second graders about magnets, showing how they pick up nails and bits of iron. Then she asked a question to see what the children remembered.

“My name begins with the letter M, and I pick things up. What am I?”

Little Shmueli in the front row said, “A Mommy!”

title: The Express Lane
text:
I was in the express lane at the store, quietly fuming. Completely ignoring the sign, the woman ahead of me had slipped into line with a cart piled high with groceries.

Imagine my delight when the cashier waved her forward, looked into the cart, and asked sweetly, “So which six items would you like to buy?”

title: The Biggest Fish Story
text:
Sidney and Abe were swapping fishing stories with great relish. “Once in Durban,” said Sid, “I caught a fish so big, it took three men to schlep it in!”

“That’s nothing,” said Abe. “I once caught a lamp with a date engraved on it: 1492, when Columbus discovered America!”

“Big deal,” said Sid, rising from his chair. “My fish weighed a hundred and fifty pounds.”

“Yeah? Well, the lamp I caught was still lit!”

They stared each other down, nose to nose, until Sid said, “Listen, Abe. How about I make my fish five pounds, and you put your light out?”

title: Back on His Feet
text:
“How is your uncle doing since the operation?”

“Great. His broken leg has healed, and he’s using it as if nothing happened. The doctor said he’d have him walking within a month.”

“Wonderful that he’s walking again!”

“Yes. Then the doctor sent the bill, and he had to sell his car to pay it. That’s why he’s walking.”

title: The Union Meeting
text:
Max, the head of the workers’ committee at a state-owned company in Israel, addressed a union meeting. “Comrades! We’ve agreed on a new deal with management. We will no longer work five days a week.”

“Hooray!” cheered the crowd.

“We will finish at 3 instead of 4.” “Hooray!” “We will start at 9 instead of 7.” “Hooray!” “We will get a 150 percent raise.” “Hooray!”

“And we will only work on Wednesdays.”

Silence. Then a voice from the back: “Every Wednesday?”

title: No Refills
text:
A distraught senior citizen phoned her doctor’s office. “Is it true,” she asked, “that the medication you prescribed has to be taken for the rest of my life?”

“I’m afraid so,” said the doctor.

There was a moment of silence. “Then I wonder how serious my condition is,” she said, “because this prescription says ‘No refills.’”

title: The Lucky Saucer
text:
A famous art collector was walking through town when he noticed a mangy cat lapping milk from a saucer in a shop doorway. He recognized the saucer: extremely old and very valuable.

He strolled in and offered two dollars for the cat. “Sorry, the cat isn’t for sale.” He explained that he needed a cat to catch mice and raised the offer to twenty dollars. “Sold,” said the owner.

“For twenty bucks,” said the collector, “could you throw in that old saucer? The cat is used to it, and it saves me buying a dish.”

“Sorry, buddy,” said the owner. “That’s my lucky saucer. So far this week I’ve sold sixty-eight cats.”

title: We Need Ten
text:
A famous football coach was on vacation with his family in Maine. When they walked into a movie theater and sat down, the handful of people there began to applaud. He thought, “I can’t believe it! People recognize me all the way up here.”

Then a man came over and said, “Thanks so much for coming. They won’t start the movie unless there are at least ten of us.”

title: What’s in the Truck?
text:
A farmer was driving down the road with a load of fertilizer. A little boy playing in front of his house called out, “What have you got in your truck?”

“Fertilizer,” said the farmer.

“What are you going to do with it?”

“Put it on strawberries.”

“You ought to live here,” the little boy advised. “We put sugar and cream on ours.”

title: The Red Duck
text:
A kindergarten teacher handed out a coloring page of a duck holding an umbrella. "Color the duck yellow and the umbrella green," she said.

Little Bobby colored his duck bright red. "Bobby," said the teacher, "how many red ducks have you ever seen?"

"Exactly as many as I've seen ducks holding umbrellas," said Bobby.

title: A Very Helpful Lawyer
text:
A man was told by his doctor that his time was short, so he hurried to a lawyer to write his will. Three minutes later he stormed out of the office.

"What happened?" asked the secretary.

"That man is crazy!" he fumed. "I told him I wanted to make a will, and he said, 'Fine, just answer a few questions and then leave everything to me.'"

title: The Two-Dollar Hearing Aid
text:
A man needed a hearing aid but didn't want to spend much. "How much are they?" he asked.

"From two dollars to two thousand," said the salesman.

"I'll take the two-dollar model."

The salesman hung it around his neck. "Put this button in your ear and run the string down to your pocket."

"And how does it work?"

"For two dollars, it doesn't," said the salesman. "But when people see it, they'll talk louder."

title: The Rabbi and the Peanuts
text:
The rabbi paid a visit to an elderly woman from the shul. On her coffee table sat a big bowl of peanuts. "May I have a few?" he asked.

"Of course!" she said.

They chatted for an hour, and when he stood to leave he noticed the bowl was nearly empty. "Forgive me, I only meant to take a few!"

"Don't worry," she said. "Since I lost my teeth, all I can do is suck the chocolate off them."

(They were chocolate-covered peanuts.)

title: A Call for the Dog
text:
A telemarketer phoned a house. "May I speak with Max, please?"

"I suppose that's possible," said the man who answered, "but it's rather strange."

"Why is that?"

"Because this is the first time anyone has ever called for the dog."

title: Yankel Returns the Purse
text:
A thief walked into the rabbi's study with a purse full of money. "I found this in the street," he said. "Please help me find the owner."

After he left, the rabbi noticed that his gold watch was gone. His assistant tracked the man down, and sure enough, the watch was in his pocket.

"I don't understand," said the rabbi. "You return a purse full of money and then steal my watch?"

"Rabbi," said Yankel, "finding a purse, I have a mitzvah to return it. Stealing? That's my business."

title: Good News, Bad News
text:
An artist asked the gallery owner whether anyone had shown interest in his paintings.

"I have good news and bad news," said the owner. "A gentleman asked whether your work would go up in value after your death. I told him it would, and he bought all fifteen paintings."

"Wonderful!" said the artist. "So what's the bad news?"

"The man was your doctor."

title: Smarter Than Einstein
text:
After the sermon, a congregant shook the rabbi's hand. "Rabbi, you must be smarter than Einstein!"

The rabbi glowed. But all week he wondered why anyone would say such a thing, so the next Shabbat he asked the man what he meant.

"Well, Rabbi," the man explained, "they say Einstein was so brilliant that only ten people in the whole world could understand him. But nobody understands you."

title: One for You, One for Me
text:
Two boys sat behind the cemetery wall, dividing a bucket of nuts. "One for you, one for me. One for you, one for me."

A man passing by heard the voices and froze. He grabbed an old man with a cane. "Quick! Angels are inside, dividing up the souls!"

They crept up to the wall and listened. "One for you, one for me..." Then a voice said, "That's all. Now let's get the ones by the fence."

They say the old man got back to town five minutes ahead of the younger one.

title: Digging for Ancient Wires
text:
French archaeologists dug a thousand meters down and found copper wire. "Our ancestors had a telephone network!" they announced.

The English dug two thousand meters and found fiber-optic cable. "Our ancestors had a digital network before the French!"

The Israelis dug five thousand meters in a Jerusalem market and found absolutely nothing. Their conclusion: "Five thousand years ago, our ancestors were already wireless."

title: The Hat in the Flood
text:
During a flood, a girl and a boy sat on a rooftop watching things float past. An old hat drifted by, then turned around and came back, then drifted away again, and returned again.

"Look at that hat!" said the girl. "Down the river, back again, down, back..."

"Oh, that's nothing," said the boy. "That's my dad. This morning Mom told him that come hell or high water, he was mowing the lawn today."

title: I'll Start in Three Months
text:
Harry went for a job interview, and it went well. "We'd like to hire you," they said. "We'll pay ten dollars an hour now, and in three months we'll raise it to fifteen. When can you start?"

"In three months," said Harry.

title: All Twelve of You?
text:
After a year-long murder trial, the district attorney stared in disbelief as the jury read its verdict: not guilty.

"What possible reason could you have for acquitting him?" he asked bitterly.

"Insanity," said the foreman.

"All twelve of you?"

title: Five Sets of Teeth
text:
In 1936 a dentist named Morris fled Germany with five sets of solid gold teeth, bought with all his savings. In New York, the customs officer asked why on earth he needed five sets.

"Jews who keep kosher have separate dishes for meat and dairy," said Morris. "I'm so careful, I have separate teeth too."

"That's two. And the other three?"

"For Passover, of course, meat and dairy again."

"Four. And the fifth?"

"Sometimes," Morris sighed, "I like to eat treif!"

title: Dancing on the Grave
text:
A drill sergeant finished chewing out a cadet. As he walked away he said, "I suppose when I die, you'll come and dance on my grave."

"Not me, Sarge," said the cadet. "When I get out of the Army, I promised myself I'd never stand in line again."

title: Erev Bankruptcy
text:
Lionel stormed into the bank. "What is this threatening letter?"

"Mr. Levy, your account didn't have enough money to cover your checks. Why didn't you deposit the funds first, as you always do?"

"I couldn't. It was a Jewish holy day."

"I know many Jewish customers," said the manager, "and I thought I knew all the holy days. Which one?"

"Erev Bankruptcy," said Lionel. (Erev means "the eve of.")

title: Thursday Afternoon, Two Years From Now
text:
After saving for twenty years, Morris ordered a car and was told it would arrive in two years. At the door he turned back. "Which week exactly?"

The salesman checked. "That week."

Morris turned back again. "And what day?"

"Thursday," said the salesman, a little annoyed.

At the door once more: "Morning or afternoon?"

"Afternoon!" snapped the salesman.

"Thank goodness," said Morris. "The plumber is coming in the morning."

title: Squeezing the Lemon
text:
A pub offered $1,000 to anyone who could squeeze one more drop out of a lemon after its mighty barman had wrung it dry. Weightlifters and wrestlers had all failed.

One day a scrawny little man in thick glasses stepped up. The crowd laughed. The barman squeezed the lemon and handed over the wrinkled rind.

The little man clenched his fist, and four more drops fell into the glass. The crowd went silent. The barman paid up and asked, "What do you do? Are you a strongman?"

"No," said the little man. "I raise funds for charity."

title: The General Has Told a Joke
text:
A general lectured to a group of foreign officers and spent three minutes telling his favorite joke. His interpreter translated it in about eight words, and the whole room burst into laughter.

Afterward the general asked, "How did you translate such a long joke so quickly?"

"Well, sir," said the interpreter, "I didn't think they would get the point, so I said: 'The general has just told a joke. Please laugh.'"

title: Scared or Apprehensive?
text:
During a night exercise, a paratrooper sat next to a young lieutenant who looked rather pale.

"Scared, lieutenant?"

"No," said the lieutenant. "Apprehensive."

"What's the difference?"

"None. It just sounds better."

title: The Early Bird Special
text:
Shlomo and Yetta were getting ready for dinner. "Darling," said Yetta, "should I wear the blue suit or the green dress?"

"Whatever you like," said Shlomo.

"Should I wear my gold watch or my pearls?"

"Either one is fine."

"And the small earrings or the big ones?"

"Yetta," said Shlomo, "pick something already! We're going to miss the Early Bird Special!"

title: Just Tell a Lie
text:
At a party, a gentleman met a woman he knew and, as politeness required, told her how lovely she looked. She wasn't a diplomat. "I wish I could say the same about you," she answered.

Without missing a beat he replied, "Why not? Do what I do. Tell a lie!"

title: Where Do the Copies Come Out?
text:
The CEO stood in front of the paper shredder, looking puzzled.

"Need help?" asked a passing secretary.

"Yes, how does this thing work?"

"Simple," she said, and fed his thick report into it.

"Thanks," said the CEO. "But where do the copies come out?"

title: Watch Your Overcoat
text:
A crowded cafeteria had a sign: "Watch Your Hat and Overcoat." Meyer took it seriously. He kept turning around every minute, nearly choking on his food.

His friend Moishe calmly kept eating. Finally Moishe said, "You fool, stop watching our coats!"

"I'm only watching mine," said Meyer. "Yours has been gone for half an hour."

title: Ten Minutes to Say It All
text:
A famous writer was master of ceremonies at a literary evening. He asked a professor of English literature to keep his remarks to ten minutes.

"Ten minutes!" protested the professor. "How can I possibly tell them everything I know about English literature in ten minutes?"

"Sir," said the writer, "I advise you to speak very slowly."

title: The Toothbrush Salesman
text:
On Monday the children reported on their weekend assignment: sell something. Mary sold cookies and made $30. Sally sold magazines and made $45.

Then Johnny dumped a box of cash on the teacher's desk. "Two thousand, four hundred and sixty-seven dollars!"

"What did you sell?"

"Toothbrushes."

"How could you sell that many toothbrushes?"

"I found the busiest corner in town and set up a chocolate chip cookie stand with free samples. Everyone said, 'This tastes like mud!' And I said, 'It is. Want to buy a toothbrush?'"

title: What Does Your Daddy Do?
text:
Two little boys met on the jungle gym.

"I'm Moishe," said the first. "What's your name?"

"Dovid."

"My daddy's an accountant. What does your daddy do?"

"My daddy's a lawyer."

"An honest one?" asked Moishe.

"No," said Dovid. "The regular kind."

title: The Dog Died Years Ago
text:
"James," said the Duchess, "how long have you been with us?"

"About thirty years, ma'am."

"My records say you were hired to look after the dog."

"Yes, ma'am."

"James, that dog died twenty-seven years ago!"

"Yes, ma'am," said James. "What would you like me to do now?"

title: A Ski Holiday
text:
Abe came home and gathered the family. "I'm tired of work, committees and obligations. I'm going on a SKI holiday!"

"For how long?" asked his daughter.

"As long as it takes."

"Tatte, what is a SKI holiday?"

Her father smiled. "Spending the Kids' Inheritance!"

title: I Can't Hear You, Melvyn
text:
Benny was vacationing at a five-star hotel when the operator called. "Mr. Levy, your brother-in-law Melvyn is on the line. He says it's urgent."

"Put him through."

"Benny, I'm in trouble with the tax people. I need you to send them $25,000 today!"

"I can't hear you, Melvyn. Something is wrong with the hotel phone."

"I NEED $25,000!"

"Sorry, I still can't hear you."

Then the operator cut in: "Mr. Levy, I can hear him perfectly."

Benny shouted into the phone, "Then why don't YOU send him the $25,000?"

title: Why Bring the Horse?
text:
A man hired a wagon and driver for a trip. At the first steep hill, the driver said, "Everybody out, we have to help the horse pull." At the top, "Everybody out, we must help the horse go down slowly." This happened again and again.

At last they arrived, tired and covered in dust. The passenger said, "I understand why you made the trip. It's your livelihood. And I know why I came. But tell me, why did we need to bring the horse?"

title: If He Hadn't Been Sick
text:
Union talks were stuck. The union insisted nobody was abusing sick leave. One morning the company's negotiator held up the newspaper. "This man called in sick yesterday!"

On the sports page was a photo of the worker, who had just won a local golf tournament with an excellent score.

The room was silent until a union negotiator said, "Wow. Imagine what he would have scored if he hadn't been sick!"

title: Which Group Goes First?
text:
An airman at an induction center sold insurance to nearly every new recruit. His captain stood at the back to hear the pitch.

"If you have insurance and something happens to you," said the airman, "the government pays your family $200,000. If you don't, it pays only $6,000. So which group do you think they'll send out first?"

title: Pick Up the Pen
text:
At a childbirth class, the husbands were given bags of sand to wear so they could feel what pregnancy is like. One husband shrugged. "This isn't so bad."

The instructor dropped a pen. "Please pick it up."

"You mean the way my wife would do it?" he asked.

"Exactly."

To the delight of the other husbands, he turned to his wife and said, "Honey, would you pick up that pen for me?"

title: The Talking Dog for Sale
text:
A man driving through the countryside saw a sign: "Talking Dog for Sale." The owner sent him to the backyard, where a Labrador sat waiting.

"You talk?" asked the man.

"Sure," said the dog. "I was recruited by the CIA as a young pup. For eight years I flew around the world listening in on spies and world leaders, because nobody suspects a dog. Then I worked airport security and earned a pile of medals. Now I'm retired with a wife and a houseful of puppies."

Astonished, the man asked the owner, "How much for the dog?"

"Ten dollars."

"Ten?! He's amazing! Why so cheap?"

"Because he's a liar. He never did any of that."

title: It's for My Wife
text:
At a dinner party, a wife whispered to her husband, "That's your third trip to the dessert table! The hostess must think you're a glutton."

"I don't think so," he said. "I told her it's for you."

title: Landing in the Roses
text:
A man was fixing his roof when he slipped and fell, shouting, "Help! Somebody call a doctor!"

His neighbor ran over. "Relax! You landed in the bushes. You don't need a doctor."

"Yes I do," groaned the man. "When my wife sees what I did to her roses, I'll need serious medical attention."

title: Put Down Yes
text:
A groom and his bride-to-be met with the rabbi to fill out the paperwork for the wedding. The groom read the questions aloud. The last one was: "Are you entering this marriage of your own free will?"

He wasn't sure what to say and looked at his fiancée.

"Put down yes," she said.

title: A Portrait With Jewelry
text:
An elderly woman asked an artist to paint her portrait. "Paint me with diamond earrings, a pearl necklace, emerald bracelets and a ruby brooch."

"But you're not wearing any of those," said the artist.

"I know," she said. "If I die before my husband, he'll surely remarry right away. I want the new wife to go crazy looking for the jewelry."

title: Perfect Eyesight
text:
Arthur, ninety, had played golf every day since retiring. One day he came home gloomy. "I'm giving up golf. My eyes are so bad I can't see where the ball goes."

His wife said, "Take my brother along. He's a hundred and three, but his eyesight is perfect."

The next day Arthur teed off and squinted down the fairway. "Did you see where it went?"

"Of course," said the brother. "My eyes are perfect."

"So where is it?"

"I don't remember."

title: A Nice Surprise
text:
Avraham went into a department store and headed straight for the perfume counter. "Today is my wife's birthday, and I'd like a nice bottle of French perfume."

"What a lovely surprise for her," said the clerk.

"It certainly will be," said Avraham. "She's expecting a diamond necklace."

title: Maybe I Bring You Bad Luck?
text:
Chaim lay in the hospital recovering from a heart attack, with his wife Yenta at his side. Slowly he came around. "Yenta, remember my appendix operation?"

"Of course."

"You sat by my bed."

"Where else would I be?"

"And the emergency hernia surgery, when I almost didn't make it?"

"I was there," said Yenta, wiping a tear.

"And now a heart attack, and again you're by my side." Chaim frowned. "Yenta, maybe you bring me bad luck?"

title: The Doctor Says I Have a Flucky
text:
An elderly man was bumped by a car crossing the street. He seemed fine, but his wife sent him to the doctor just in case. At home she asked, "Nu, what did the doctor say?"

"He says I have a flucky."

"Oy! A flucky! What do you do for a flucky?"

"I forgot to ask."

She ran to the neighbors. One said, "Cold! Ice is the only cure for a flucky." Another said, "Cold? Heat! Never cold!"

Frantic, the wife called the doctor. "What exactly does my husband have?"

"Nothing," said the doctor. "I told him he got off lucky."

title: Say, How Nice
text:
Four women sat over coffee, comparing what their husbands had bought them: a fur coat, a sports car, a summer villa. After each one, Mrs. Levy said, "How nice."

Finally they turned to her. "And what did your husband buy you?"

"He sent me to a course on etiquette."

"And what did you learn?"

"When people talk nonsense, to say, 'How nice.'"

title: Aqua-Thermal Treatment
text:
I asked a friend what he was up to. "I'm working on aqua-thermal treatment of ceramics and steel in a controlled environment."

I was very impressed. Then I asked a few more questions and discovered he was washing the dishes, with hot water, under his wife's supervision.

title: Hand Over the Wallet
text:
It was John's turn to drive the carpool, and a new rider had joined. As they drove, John grew suspicious of him. He checked his coat on the seat between them, and his wallet wasn't there.

He slammed on the brakes. "Out! And hand over the wallet!"

The frightened passenger handed over a wallet, and John drove off, leaving him on the roadside.

That evening John told his wife the whole story. "Oh, that reminds me," she said. "You left your wallet at home this morning."

title: You Didn't Miss a Thing
text:
It was Passover, and I had planned to spend it watching football. My wife had other plans, and I found myself at the family Seder. When the coast was clear, I slipped away and switched on the game.

A few minutes later my wife brought me a cup of coffee. "What's the score?"

"Nothing to nothing at the end of the third quarter."

"See?" she said. "You didn't miss a thing."

title: One Missing Letter
text:
Let me tell you, friends: one small typo can make your life miserable. While away on a fishing trip, I texted my wife a short, romantic note and left out one tiny letter.

Now I need police protection to enter my own house. I wrote: "Hi darling, I'm having the best time of my whole life, and I wish you were her!"

title: He Thinks He Knows You
text:
Max and Selma were driving across the country, with Selma at the wheel, when a patrolman pulled them over. "Ma'am, do you know you were speeding?"

Selma, who was hard of hearing, asked Max, "What did he say?"

"He says you were speeding!"

"May I see your license?"

"What did he say?"

"He wants to see your license!"

The officer looked at it. "New York? I spent time there once. I went on a blind date with the most annoying woman I ever met."

"What did he say?" asked Selma.

"He says he thinks he knows you!"

title: Profit From Another's Mistake
text:
Morris went to his rabbi with a question. "Rabbi, is it proper for one man to profit from another man's mistake?"

"No, Morris. It is not."

"Are you sure?"

"Absolutely sure."

"Then, Rabbi," said Morris, "how about returning the two hundred dollars I paid you for marrying me to my wife?"

title: We Also Deliver
text:
Moshe, who owned a small kosher deli, was questioned by a tax agent about his return. He had reported an $80,000 profit.

"Why won't you people leave me alone?" said Moshe. "I work like a dog, my whole family helps, and we close only three days a year!"

"It's not your income that bothers us," said the agent. "It's the travel deductions: ten trips to Israel for you and your wife."

Moshe smiled. "Oh, that. Well... we also deliver."

title: Looking Into the Crib
text:
One night a wife found her husband standing over their newborn's crib. She watched silently as emotions crossed his face: wonder, doubt, delight, amazement.

Deeply touched, she slipped her arms around him. "A penny for your thoughts," she whispered.

"It's amazing," he said. "How can anyone build a crib like that for only $46.50?"

title: The Anniversary Wish
text:
Sadie and Harry were celebrating their thirty-second anniversary at a quiet restaurant when a tiny fairy appeared on their table. "For being such a devoted couple, I'll grant each of you a wish."

"I'd like to travel the world with my darling husband," said Sadie. Poof! Two tickets for a luxury cruise appeared.

Harry thought for a moment. "This is very romantic, but a chance like this won't come again. I'm sorry, my love, but I wish for a wife thirty years younger."

The fairy waved her wand, and poof! Harry was ninety-two.

title: Never in the Front Seat
text:
After golf, Sam's car wouldn't start, and the only ride home was with Goldberg, a man Sam couldn't stand because he never stopped bragging. "Glad to help," said Goldberg. "And you'll get to ride in my new Rolls-Royce!"

Sam admired all the gadgets. "What's this?"

"My GPS."

"And these numbers?"

"The on-board computer," said Goldberg, and added smugly, "I take it you've never been in a Rolls-Royce before?"

"Oh, I have," said Sam. "Just never in the front seat."

title: David Is an Antique Dealer
text:
Sharon and Tessa met for coffee. "How are things?" asked Tessa.

"Not good," said Sharon. "I don't think Steven finds me attractive anymore. The older I get, the less he looks at me."

"I'm so sorry," said Tessa. "My David says I get more beautiful every year."

"Yes," said Sharon, "but don't forget, David is an antique dealer!"

title: A Small Deposit
text: Shelley was walking past a jewelry store when a diamond bracelet caught her eye. She went in. "Excuse me," she asked the saleswoman, "would a small deposit hold that bracelet until my husband does something unforgivable?"

title: The Quiet Burglar
text:
A man went to the police station and asked to speak with the burglar who had broken into his house the night before.

"You'll get your chance in court," said the desk sergeant.

"No, no," said the man. "I want to know how he got in without waking my wife. I've been trying to do that for years!"

title: Pastrami Sandwiches
text:
The air-raid siren sounded in Haifa, and a woman rushed down to the shelter. Halfway there she noticed her husband wasn't behind her.

"Sidney, come on!"

"One minute! I have to get my teeth!"

"Never mind your teeth!" she shouted. "What do you think they're dropping, pastrami sandwiches?"

title: I Don't Have to Laugh
text:
The boss came back from lunch in a good mood and gathered the staff to hear a few jokes he'd picked up. Everyone laughed uproariously, except one young woman.

"What's the matter?" said the boss. "No sense of humor?"

"I don't have to laugh," she said. "I'm leaving on Friday."

title: Three Doctors Already
text:
At ten at night the phone rang at Dr. Cohen's house. "It's Dr. Goldberg," said his wife. "I hope it isn't another emergency."

"Don't worry, everything's fine," said Dr. Goldberg. "I'm here with Dr. Katz and Dr. Schwartz. We're playing poker and we need a fourth. Want to join us?"

"Yes, of course," said Dr. Cohen gravely. "I'm leaving now."

"What happened?" his wife asked.

"It's very serious," said Dr. Cohen. "They've already called three doctors."

title: I Do Not Know the Time
text:
Yossi, exhausted after a twenty-hour shift, was locked out of his Tel Aviv apartment, so he parked on a quiet street and fell asleep. It happened to be a popular jogging route.

A knock on the window woke him. "Do you have the time?" a jogger asked. "Five-thirty," said Yossi. Soon another knock: "Five forty-five."

To get some peace, Yossi wrote a sign and stuck it on his window: "I DO NOT KNOW THE TIME."

He dozed off. Then another knock. A jogger leaned in and said, "It's six o'clock, by the way."

title: Three on a Motorbike
text:
A traffic cop spots two young yeshiva students on a motorbike, tzitzit (ritual fringes) fluttering in the wind, and decides to follow them. For half an hour he waits for a mistake. They stop at every red light, keep under the speed limit and signal every turn.

Finally he pulls them over and checks their licenses, their insurance, everything. All in order. Baffled, he says, "In all my years I have never met two boys on a motorbike who did nothing wrong. How is that possible?"

"Oh," they smile, "G-d is with us."

"Aha!" says the cop, writing out a ticket. "That makes three on a bike."

title: A Visitor Down the Chimney
text:
A burglar climbs down the chimney of a house in the middle of the night, and lands in the rabbi's study. The rabbi is sitting up, learning Torah.

The rabbi looks up and says calmly, "Yankel, what are you doing here?"

The burglar thinks fast. "Rabbi," he says, "I have a shailah, a question of Jewish law."

"Go ahead," says the rabbi.

"How does a man get out of here?"

title: A Dollar for Israel
text:
A man walks into a bakery and asks for a bagel. "That will be twenty dollars," says the baker. "Twenty?!" "A dollar for the bagel and nineteen for Israel." Not wanting to seem stingy, the man pays.

Before Shabbat he returns for a challah. Forty dollars. Again, he pays.

On Monday he orders a cheesecake. Seventy dollars. This time he has had enough. "This is ridiculous! I want to speak to the owner!"

"Sure," says the baker, and calls toward the back office, "Israel! A customer wants to talk to you!"

title: Whose Phone Is This?
text:
Several men are changing in a golf club locker room when a cell phone rings on a bench. One man answers on speaker, and everyone listens.

"Honey, I'm at the mall. I found a beautiful leather coat for only $1,000. May I buy it?"

"Sure, if you love it."

"And I stopped by the car dealer. There's a new model I adore. $60,000."

"Fine, but get it with all the options."

"Also, that house we liked last year is back on the market, for $950,000."

"Offer them $900,000."

"Wonderful! I love you!" "I love you too."

He hangs up. The other men stare at him, amazed. He holds up the phone and asks, "Does anyone know whose phone this is?"

title: Call Me Anything
text:
Seymour Kaplan, a New York tailor, saved up for a trip to the Russian town where he was born. He had no passport, so he bought one for $15 from a fellow who "knew about such things." "Remember," the man warned, "your name is now Isaac Leibovitch. Forget your own name and you'll be fine."

Seymour repeated it all the way to the border. There, a stern official studied the photo, studied Seymour, and asked, "Name?"

Seymour was so nervous that his mind went blank. "My name... my name is... well, I..."

"Come now, surely you know your own name!"

"Mister," Seymour pleaded, "call me anything you want, but please, don't call me Seymour Kaplan!"

title: Anything Less Expensive?
text:
A jewelry store manager catches a shoplifter with a necklace. "Listen," says the thief, "you don't want trouble and neither do I. How about I just buy the necklace and we forget this ever happened?" The manager agrees and writes up the sale.

"You know," says the thief, "this is more than I wanted to spend. Do you have anything less expensive?"

We say we want to do teshuvah, to return and make things right. But real change has a price, and we have to be willing to pay it.

title: Who Gets to Blow the Shofar
text:
The shul president tells the rabbi, "Mr. Goldberg will donate $10,000 to the shul if he may blow the shofar on the High Holy Days." The rabbi agrees.

But on Rosh Hashanah, the rabbi takes the shofar and blows it himself. The president and Goldberg are furious and rush over. "Don't worry," says the rabbi, "Mr. Goldberg will blow on Yom Kippur."

"But on Yom Kippur we only blow once, at the very end!" says Goldberg.

"Fool," whispers the president. "Once the shofar is in your hand, who's going to stop you?"

title: Nothing New to Say
text:
A philosophy professor is invited to lecture in China, and brings an interpreter. "Stop after every sentence?" the interpreter asks. "No," says the professor. "When I see you shake your head, then stop."

The professor speaks for fifteen minutes. The interpreter says four words in Chinese. Fifteen minutes later, four more words. Then again, and again, until the lecture ends and the audience files out.

Amazed, the professor asks, "How did you summarize so much in so few words?"

"Simple," says the interpreter. "After fifteen minutes I told them, 'He has said nothing new.' After the next, 'Still nothing new.' Then, 'I don't think he will say anything new.' And at the end I said, 'I was right.'"

title: The Bet About Questions
text:
A very proud scholar makes a bet with a simple fellow. "For every question I ask that you can't answer, you pay me $5. For every question you ask that I can't answer, I pay you $5,000." "Okay," says the fellow.

"How many continents are there?" asks the scholar. The fellow doesn't know, and pays $5.

"Now me," he says. "What stands on two legs but sleeps on three?"

The scholar thinks and thinks, and finally pays $5,000. "I give up. What's the answer?"

The fellow quietly hands him $5.

title: I Wish I Had a Dozen
text:
A woman walks into an elegant hat shop and tries on hat after hat. One is too big, one too wide, another too fancy. Finally the exhausted saleswoman says sweetly, "I wish I had a dozen customers like you," and walks to the back of the store.

A colleague, who overheard, is puzzled. "Why on earth did you say that?"

"Because," says the saleswoman through gritted teeth, "I have a hundred like her, and I wish I only had a dozen."

title: Cohen and O'Reilly
text:
Moshe is walking down Broadway when he notices a little tailor shop with a sign: COHEN AND O'REILLY. He steps inside and says to the tailor behind the counter, "What a heartwarming thing! A Jew and an Irishman working side by side!"

The tailor seems unmoved. "You're surprised by this?"

"Well, yes!" says Moshe. "Cohen and O'Reilly in one shop!"

"So here's another surprise for you," says the tailor. "I'm O'Reilly."

title: Everything Is Faster in China
text:
A tourist from China lands at Ben Gurion Airport and takes a taxi to Tel Aviv. Passing some buses, he says, "Your buses are so slow. In China, buses are very fast." The driver says nothing.

They pass a train. "Your train is slow. In China, trains are very fast." The driver says nothing.

In Tel Aviv he watches people walking. "Everyone walks so slowly. In China, people walk very fast." Still nothing.

At the hotel the driver says, "That's 500 shekels."

"What?!" says the tourist. "In Israel the buses are slow, the trains are slow, the people are slow. Why is the meter the only thing that's fast?"

"Because," says the driver, "it was made in China."

title: The Good News and the Bad News
text:
A New York train with two engines is driven by a recent immigrant from Israel, Itzik. Partway along, one engine breaks down. "No problem," says Itzik, and carries on at half power. Further on, the second engine dies, and the train grinds to a halt.

Itzik makes an announcement. "Ladies and gentlemen, I have good news and bad news. The bad news is that both engines have failed and we'll be here a while. The good news is that you didn't decide to fly."

title: A Policeman With a Dog
text:
Bubbe Silver comes home to find her house has been burgled. She phones the police and demands an officer right away.

The dispatcher explains that every officer nearby is busy. The only car free is the one with the police dog. "I don't care," she says. "Send him now!"

Soon the car arrives, and out steps an officer with a German shepherd on a leash. Bubbe throws up her hands. "Oy gevalt! My house is robbed, and they send me a blind policeman!"

title: The Maggid and the Goat
text:
A maggid, a traveling preacher, gives a talk in a village. Most of the listeners doze off, but one man seems to follow every word, nodding and shaking his head at just the right moments.

Afterward the maggid goes over, delighted. "I'm so glad you enjoyed my talk!"

"To be honest," says the man, "I didn't understand a word. But with that beard you look just like my goat, and I was arguing with myself whether you're related."

title: Peas in the Shoes
text:
Two yeshiva students are caught by their rabbi doing things they shouldn't, even before Shabbat had ended. The next day he calls them in. They confess and accept that they deserve a punishment.

The rabbi goes to his kitchen and returns with two bags of dried peas. "Put these in your shoes and walk on them for a week, to remember how hard life is when you stray from the Torah."

A few days later the two meet. One is limping badly, with dark circles under his eyes. The other is walking along happily.

"How are you walking so freely? Didn't you put the peas in your shoes?"

"Of course I did," says the other. "How could I disobey the rabbi?" He walks off, then turns around. "But I boiled them first."

title: The Teacher and the Tie
text:
A teacher hurt his back and wore a plaster cast under his shirt, invisible to anyone. On the first day of term he was assigned the most rowdy class in school.

He walked in calmly, opened the window wide and sat down at his desk. The class grew noisy, and he scolded them. Meanwhile the strong breeze kept flapping his tie. He kept fixing it, while the class grew wilder.

Finally he lost patience with the tie, picked up a big stapler and stapled it to his chest, several times.

Discipline was never a problem again.

title: Mama Goes Shopping
text:
Mama goes shopping and examines everything.

"I don't like the look of this codfish." "Lady, for looks you buy goldfish, not codfish."

"Oy, this chicken has a broken leg." "Lady, are you going to eat it or dance with it?"

"Before you weigh the meat, take out the bones." "Lady, I buy with bones, you buy with bones." "I won't pay for bones." "All right, no bones."

"Thank you, you're a gentleman. Now put the bones in a separate bag for soup. And never mind the meat. I don't like your meat anyway."

title: A Raise at Last
text:
Yankel asks his boss for a raise. "Sir, I've worked here more than ten years. I have three companies after me, but I came to you first."

"I'd love to give you a raise," says the boss, "but times are hard."

"I know sales are down," says Yankel, "but please consider my hard work and loyalty over a whole decade."

"All right, I don't want to lose you. Ten percent more, and five extra vacation days."

"It's a deal! Thank you!"

"Just curious," says the boss, "which three companies were after you?"

"The electric company, the gas company and the water company!"

title: How Long Have You Been Waiting?
text:
A company runs tours of the historic district, with guides in colonial costume. One guide trips and breaks his wrist, and goes to the hospital in full 18th-century outfit.

He sits in the waiting room. A policeman walks by, does a double take at the three-cornered hat and buckled shoes, and asks, "Just how long have you been waiting?"

title: The Pain Is in My Chest
text:
A man complains of chest pains. His wife tells him to lie down while she calls the doctor. The doctor arrives, sits at the bedside and takes the man's hand to check his pulse.

"Doctor," the patient says weakly, "it's not my hand. The pain is in my chest, near my heart."

"I know very well," says the doctor. "But from the hand we know how the heart is doing."

title: When Will You Be Six?
text:
A mother tells her little boy, while they wait for the bus, "Tell the driver you're five, and you'll ride for free."

They board. The driver asks, "How old are you?"

"I'm five," says the boy proudly.

The driver has a son that age and smiles. "And when will you be six?"

"When I get off the bus," says the boy.

title: The Safari Bar Mitzvah
text:
In a small town, a group of families were each trying to throw a grander bar or bat mitzvah party than the last. One booked the Waldorf Astoria. The next chartered a plane to London. The next rented a yacht for an all-day cruise.

The last family despaired, since everything had been done. Then the mother had an idea: a safari bar mitzvah! They flew to Kenya, where a line of elephants was waiting. Guests and luggage were loaded on, the bar mitzvah boy up front with the guide, and Dad bringing up the rear.

Thirty minutes into the jungle, the procession stopped. Dad checked his watch, galloped up front and asked the guide, "What's the holdup?"

"We have to wait," said the guide, "for the bat mitzvah party ahead of us."

title: The Hadassah Ladies
text:
A tour bus carrying thirty Hadassah ladies overturns, and they all arrive in Heaven. But the computers at the gates are down, so they must wait. G-d arranges for them to stay temporarily somewhere warmer.

A few hours later G-d gets an urgent call from Satan. "Please take these women back! They've ruined my whole operation. They've been here only a few hours and already raised $100,000 for air conditioning!"

title: G-d Was Busy
text:
A professor tells his college class he will prove there is no G-d. "G-d, if You're real, knock me off this platform. I'll give You fifteen minutes!"

Ten minutes pass. "Here I am, G-d, still waiting..."

In the last minute, a huge rugby player walks past the door, hears the professor, strides in and sends him flying off the platform.

The shaken professor gets up. "Who are you? Why did you do that?"

"G-d was busy," says the player. "He sent me."

title: Scream a Little Louder
text:
A dentist leans over his patient and begs, "Could you do me a favor? Could you let out a few of your loudest, most painful screams?"

"Why? Doc, it doesn't hurt that much this time."

"There are so many people in the waiting room, and I don't want to miss my golf this afternoon."

title: The Bathtub Test
text:
A journalist, Morris, visits a psychiatric hospital and asks the director how they decide whether a patient should stay.

"Simple," says the director. "We fill a bathtub, then offer the patient a teaspoon, a teacup and a bucket, and ask them to empty it."

"Ah, I understand," says Morris. "A normal person would use the bucket, because it's bigger."

"No," says the director. "A normal person would pull the plug. So, Morris, would you like a room with an east view or a west view?"

title: Applied Psychology
text:
Seventeen-year-old Avraham takes a summer job delivering food for a restaurant. He brings a meal to Bernie, who pays the bill and says grudgingly, "I suppose you want a tip?"

Avraham answers politely, "That would be most appreciated, especially since the fellow who usually delivers here warned me not to expect much from you. He said I'd be lucky to get a dime."

"Well, to prove him wrong," says Bernie, "here's two dollars."

"Thank you very much. It goes into my college fund."

"Really? What will you study?"

"Applied psychology," says Avraham.

title: Sadie's Diamond Dream
text:
At nine in the morning Sadie wakes up and nudges her husband Melvin. "Oy, darling, what a lovely dream I had."

"So tell me already."

"I dreamed you gave me a beautiful five-carat diamond ring for our anniversary."

"Mazel tov on your dream."

"So what do you think it means? Our anniversary is tomorrow!"

"Be patient," says Melvin. "Tonight, when I get home, you'll know."

All day Sadie thinks of nothing but the ring. That evening Melvin hands her a small gift-wrapped package. She tears it open, and inside is a book: "Dream Interpretation for Dummies."

title: Which Steak Would You Take?
text:
Simon takes his friend John to dinner. When the steaks arrive, Simon grabs the bigger one. John is upset.

"If you had been first to choose," Simon asks, "which would you have taken?"

"The smaller one, of course," says John.

"So what are you upset about? That's what you got!"

title: The New Boss Means Business
text:
A company hires a new CEO determined to get rid of slackers. On a tour of the building, he spots a young man leaning against a wall and wants everyone to see he means business.

"How much do you make a week?" he asks.

"Four hundred. Why?"

"Wait here." The CEO returns with $1,600 in cash. "Four weeks' pay. Now get out and don't come back!"

Feeling pleased with himself, he asks the room, "Would anyone like to tell me what that goof-off did here?"

From across the room comes a voice: "He's the pizza delivery guy."

title: Soup for Baron Rothschild
text:
The fabulously wealthy Baron Rothschild stops for lunch at a little deli in the countryside. The chicken soup is delicious. Then the waiter brings the bill.

"A hundred dollars for a bowl of chicken soup?!" says the Baron. "Is chicken soup so rare around here?"

"No," says the waiter. "But Rothschilds are."

title: Rules Are Rules
text:
Hospital rules say a discharged patient must leave in a wheelchair. So when Michelle, a student nurse, hears that the patient in room 50 is going home, she brings a wheelchair. There sits Moshe, fully dressed, suitcase at his feet.

"Just hop in, and I'll wheel you downstairs."

"I can walk perfectly well, thank you."

"I'm sorry, it's the rules."

So Moshe gives in. In the elevator, Michelle asks, "Is your wife meeting you?"

"No," says Moshe. "She's still in her room, getting out of the hospital gown."

title: Sitting by the Window
text:
A man raves to his friends about the huge, juicy steak he had downtown the day before. They decide to check it out and all go together.

The waiter brings out the smallest steaks they have ever seen. The embarrassed man calls the waiter over. "Yesterday you served me a big, juicy steak! Today I bring my friends, and you serve miniatures. What is the meaning of this?"

"Yes, sir," says the waiter. "Yesterday you were sitting by the window."

title: The Angriest Passenger
text:
Rabbi Feldman misses his bus to Buffalo, where he is to officiate at a wedding. He hops on a bus to Toronto and tells the driver, "Wake me in Buffalo. I sleep very deeply, so you must really shake me. Hundreds of people are counting on me." He repeats it twice. The driver promises.

The rabbi wakes up in the morning and looks out the window. Toronto! He storms off the bus, shouting that his trip is wasted and hundreds are waiting in vain. The driver apologizes.

A fellow driver has watched the scene. "That's the angriest passenger I've ever seen!"

"You should have seen the guy I pushed off in Buffalo," says the driver.

title: Five Hundred Lines
text:
A woman charged with a traffic violation is asked her occupation. "I'm a schoolteacher," she says.

The judge rises from the bench, beaming. "Madam, I have waited years for a schoolteacher to appear in my court. Now sit down at that table and write 'I will not run a red light' five hundred times."

title: I Would Limp Too
text:
On his rounds, a doctor shows an X-ray to a group of medical students. "As you can see, the patient limps because his left tibia and fibula are sharply bowed."
